LECTURE: How to name a java variable
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now
[00:01] we discussed on how to create variables with the help of primitive data types and how to assign data
[00:08] or values to these variables.
[00:10] So if you see here I'm trying to use a variable name as b.
[00:14] And very similarly here I'm using a name as num.
[00:17] So you might be under the assumption we can do any name except the Java keyword with any format.
[00:24] But I want to let you know that there are certain standards that we need to follow while declaring variable
[00:30] names.
[00:31] So let's try to understand what are those standards.
[00:33] Because without knowing these standards, you may end up defining some variable names which are against
[00:39] to the standards.
[00:40] And with that, whenever someone sees your code, it clearly conveys that you're not an experienced
[00:45] developer or you don't know enough about Java.
[00:48] So to avoid such scenarios, I want to share more details about the naming conventions that we need
[00:54] to follow while defining variable names.
[00:56] Whenever we want to define a name to a variable, we are encouraged to follow the camel case approach.
[01:03] So let's try to understand what is a camel case approach.
[01:07] We all know that a variable or identifier, is simply a name that we are trying to give to a memory
[01:12] location, where we want to store a value that is supported by a given primitive data type.
[01:18] We can also give an identifier to a Java class or to a Java method and the method input parameters.
[01:24] So there are many places in Java where we can define these identifiers or variables.
[01:29] But right now, since we are focusing on primitive data types inside this section, let's try to focus
[01:34] on the Java naming conventions that we need to follow,
[01:38] while we are trying to declare variables with the help of primitive data types.
[01:43] If your variable has a single word like num or number, you can always follow the lower case alphabets.
[01:49] But sometimes your variable name may contain compound words.
[01:54] Think like you want to give a name as first name.
[01:56] In such scenario, the very first point that you need to aware is space is not allowed inside the variable
[02:02] names.
[02:03] So that's why you need to give first and name without any space.
[02:07] And at the same time, whenever you are trying to use multiple compound words inside your variable name,
[02:12] you need to always make sure the very first letter inside your variable name is starting as lower case.
[02:18] Post that every subsequent word that you are trying to append to your variable name has to start with
[02:25] a capital letter.
[02:26] So first is a word, and name is a word.
[02:29] So if I try to combine them as a variable name, the first name should be like you can see in the screen.
[02:34] So this is the firstName.
[02:35] And very similarly if I want to give a variable name as totalAmnt for the amount, I'm trying to
[02:41] use a shortcut as Amnt.
[02:43] So here total is a word and Amnt is a another word.
[02:47] So total has to be completely in small letters, whereas the second word first letter has to be in the
[02:53] capital letter.
[02:54] The same applies for isValid, numOfWords.
[02:57] So in the numOfWords you can see there are three words
[03:00] num indicates number, Of and words.
[03:03] So if I combine all these three words as a single variable name, obviously all the letters inside the
[03:09] first word has to be completely lowercase, and the second word first letter, which is O, is going
[03:15] to be capital.
[03:16] And the third word first letter, which is W, is going to be capital again.

LECTURE: Introduction to floating data types
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, we discussed about the primitive data types that are going to help us to store the whole
[00:05] numbers.
[00:06] But how about real or decimal numbers?
[00:09] To store the real numbers
[00:10] we have two primitive data types under the name floating point.
[00:14] So with the help of the data types available inside the floating point, we can store real or decimal
[00:20] numbers in Java.
[00:22] So there are two primitive data types that are going to support under this floating point.
[00:27] The very first data type is float and the second one is double.
[00:30] So there is some difference between this float and double.
[00:33] Just like how we have size difference in between int and long.
[00:37] Very similarly, in between float and double we have a size difference.
[00:41] The size of float is four bytes, whereas the size of double is eight bytes.
[00:45] Apart from the size and range of numbers supported by this data types, there is also one more difference,
[00:51] which is precision.
[00:52] We know inside fractional numbers or decimal numbers.
[00:56] We can have the decimal value even up to the 50 numbers.
[01:00] So if you are looking for a lower precision up to seven decimal digits, then you can always go with
[01:06] the float data type.
[01:08] Otherwise, if you are looking for more precision with more number of decimal values, then you can
[01:13] go with the double.
[01:15] Double is going to support that decimal values up to 15 digits, just like how other primitive data
[01:21] types hasMIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE constants.
[01:24] Very similarly, the wrapper classes of float and double data types also have these static variables,
[01:31] which we can use to understand what is the minimum value and the maximum value supported by the float
[01:38] and double data types. Inside whole numbers,
[01:41] by default, every number that you are going to write is going to act as an int value.
[01:46] If you want a specific whole number to be acting as an long value, then we need to mention the suffix
[01:53] of l, very similarly inside that decimal values
[01:57] also, by default, all your decimal values are going to act as a double data type.
[02:03] But if you want to treat a specific decimal number using float data point, then it is mandatory to
[02:10] mention the suffix f either in small case letter or in the capital case letter after your decimal number.
[02:17] Mentioning d suffix value
[02:19] for the double numbers is completely optional, even if you don't mention your Java compiler by default
[02:26] is going to consider all your decimal numbers as double only.
[02:30] In the case where you want your compiler to consider a specific decimal number as a float, then you
[02:37] should definitely mention the suffix as f after your decimal number.
[02:42] So let's try to see the examples on how we can declare floating point variables and values.
[02:48] So here you can see I'm trying to declare a variable f of type float.
[02:54] Since I want my decimal number to act as a float value, it is mandatory to mention the f suffix value
[03:02] at the end of the decimal number value.
[03:04] Very similarly, in the next variable where I'm trying to use d, I'm trying to mention the suffix with
[03:09] the capital letter F, so regardless you use small letter or capital letter, the effect is going to
[03:15] be same.
[03:16] But coming to the double, you don't have to mention any suffix, because by default all the decimal
[03:22] numbers are real
[03:23] numbers are going to be considered as a double.
[03:25] So inside all my presentations I'm not going to follow the naming standards for my variables.
[03:31] So here you can see I have used a simple variable names like f, d, a.
[03:36] Whereas when I try to give the actual demo, I will follow the naming standards because I want to keep
[03:42] my presentation as simple as possible.
[03:44] If I try to use bigger numbers sometimes it may take a lot of space inside the presentation.
[03:50] That's why please ignore the naming standards that I'm following inside my presentation.

LECTURE: Other formats supported by integer & floating data types
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, with the help of integer and floating primitive data types, we are storing the decimal
[00:07] format numbers.
[00:09] By default we humans use this decimal format to understand the numeric values, but apart from decimal format values,
[00:17] there are.
[00:17] other formats are also available inside the industry which will be used in various scenarios.
[00:23] That's why inside this lecture, let's try to learn how to store the other format numbers
[00:29] also, with the help of primitive data types available inside the Java.
[00:33] Like I said before, as of now we are using decimal number format.
[00:37] Apart from these formats, Java also supports Octal number format, Hexadecimal number format, and
[00:44] the Binary number format.
[00:46] Let me give you a very quick introduction about what are these formats. Inside the Decimal number format,
[00:51] each and every number is going to be represented from 0 to 9, whereas inside the Octal number format
[00:58] every number is going to be represented with the help of 0 to 7.
[01:02] So there will be total eight values.
[01:04] That's why we call it as Octal number format.
[01:07] Whereas in the scenario of Decimal number format there will be total ten numbers 0 to 9,

LECTURE: Type casting in Java
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Now, inside this lecture let me introduce a concept called typecasting in Java.
[00:05] So what is casting ?
[00:08] Inside Java whenever you are trying to assign a value of one primitive data type to another type, we call it as
[00:14] typecasting.
[00:15] For example, you can try to assign a float value to the int data type very similarly
[00:21] you can also try to assign an integer value to the float data type.
[00:25] So here what we are trying to do.
[00:27] We are trying to assign a value of one primitive data type to another type.
[00:32] So these kind of scenarios we call it as typecasting.
[00:35] So there are two types of casting available inside Java.
[00:38] The very first one is widening casting.
[00:41] And this one is going to happen automatically.
[00:44] That's why we call it as automatic casting or implicit casting.
[00:49] The Java compiler is not going to complain or throw an any error whenever these widening casting is
[00:55] happening.
[00:55] So what is widening casting?
[00:57] If you are trying to convert a smaller type to a larger type size, such casting, we call it as implicit
[01:04] casting or widening casting.
[01:06] Why this is done automatically is it is safe because there is no chance of losing data.
[01:12] Think like you are trying to assign a byte value to the short, so whatever byte is capable of storing
[01:18] short is also capable of storing.
[01:20] That's why byte to short will not have any chance of losing the data and similarly short to car, car to int,
[01:26] int to long, long to float, float to double.
[01:30] If you want to compare widening casting to some real life scenario, think like you're working in an company.
[01:35] Based upon your smart work,
[01:37] someone is trying to promote you to the next position.
[01:40] So in such scenarios, are you going to oppose?
[01:43] Off course not, because you will be more than happy to get promoted.
[01:47] So the same is going to happen here.
[01:49] The byte value is get promoted to the short
[01:52] or you can also promote an int value to the long data type or long value to the float data type.
[01:58] So in all these kind of scenarios, since there is no chance to lose data, the widening casting or
[02:04] implicit
[02:05] casting is going to be done by your Java compiler without any complaints.
[02:09] But if you try to do the other way, like converting a large type to a smaller size type, then we call
[02:16] that casting as narrowing casting or manual casting or explicit casting.
[02:21] Whenever you are trying to convert a large type to a smaller size type, then compiler will not accept
[02:27] because there is a chance of losing that data.
[02:30] Think like you have a float value, which is 3.14 if you're trying to convert that to a long or int,
[02:37] definitely you are going to lose that decimal values.
[02:40] You are simply going to get the whole number from the float value.
[02:44] So since there is a chance of loss of data in these kind of scenarios, the developer has to explicitly
[02:51] or manually, he has to perform the narrowing casting by following a syntax. With the narrowing casting
[02:57] syntax the developer is conveying to the Java compiler, I am fine to lose some data during the conversion
[03:04] from larger type to a smaller type, since the developer itself is fine to lose the data, the Java
[03:09] compiler is not going to complain anything.
[03:12] But if the developer is trying to simply assigning a large type value to a small size type value without
[03:18] casting, then compiler will throw an error.
[03:21] So we're going to see that in the demo.
[03:23] So narrowing casting is like a demotion.
[03:26] So someone is trying to demote you in such scenarios
[03:29] are you going to accept?
[03:30] Off course not.
[03:31] You will ask them what is the reason why you want to demote me?
[03:34] What mistake I have done?
[03:36] Only when you're satisfied with the reason, then only you're going to accept that decision.
[03:41] Very similarly, Java compiler also is not going to accept the narrowing casting by default until unless
[03:48] the developer is explicitly telling to the compiler, please do the narrowing casting and I'm fine to
[03:54] lose the data.
[03:55] I hope you are clear with these definitions.
[03:57] Now let me show you some examples.
[03:59] First, we can try to understand a implicit casting or widening casting or automatic casting.

[04:16] And here I'm trying to promote my integer to the higher data type which is double.
[04:22] So since there is no chance of losing the data, my compiler is going to be more than happy to allow
[04:28] this automatic casting.
[04:30] You can see under the int variable we are going to have the data 16, whereas under the double variable
[04:36] we are going to have 16.0.
[04:38] So there is no loss of data.
[04:40] In fact we got some extra data under the decimal points.
[04:44] So this is one of the classic example of implicit casting.

[05:04] So inside boolean we saw we are going to store false and true, and these false and true are not going
[05:09] to be supported by any of the other primitive data types.
[05:12] That's why the casting of boolean to other data types is not allowed in Java.
[05:17] I hope you are clear on implicit casting example.
[05:20] Now let's see the explicit casting or manual casting or narrowing casting.
[05:25] So here the example is,

[04:41] The JVM is not going to convert all your thousand lines of bytecode into the machine code immediately.
[04:49] It is only going to do the conversion on the fly based upon the particular method that you are trying

LECTURE: Introduction to methods in Java - Part 1
----------------------------------------

[00:00] So far we have created classes and inside the classes we have declared that Java fields.
[00:05] As a next step, we should try to define methods as well inside the Java class.
[00:11] Before we try to do that, let's try to understand what is a method in Java.
[00:15] Why should we write methods inside Java?
[00:18] We already wrote a main() method in the previous section when we were trying to execute the hello world
[00:24] example.
[00:24] So you have a basic idea on how to write a method.
[00:28] Let's try to revise the same in detail inside this lecture.
[00:32] A method which we are going to define within a Java class represents the behavior of the objects belonging
[00:38] to that particular class or the behavior of the class itself.
[00:42] In other words, these methods, they are going to serve as a named blocks of code that can be invoked
[00:49] to execute its specified actions.
[00:52] I can handle a particular business use case with a Java logic inside a method, and whatever use case
[00:59] that we are trying to handle with the method, it has to be associated with the given class at the given
[01:04] object of a particular class.
[01:06] Inside a Car class, I can define methods which are going to handle the logic related to the Car.
[01:13] I should not write the logic related to the Person or a Customer inside the Car class, though technically
[01:19] it is possible and your Java compiler is not going to complain anything about that, but it is always
[01:25] a good practice to define the business logic related to of a class or an object inside its own body.
[01:33] So that's why we are going to follow the same standards throughout this course and in the same process
[01:37] I'm assuming you will also get used to the standard.
[01:40] Once we define a method inside a class, any other class, or any other entity, they can invoke our
[01:47] method.
[01:47] In such scenarios, whatever business logic we have written inside a method will be executed.
[01:53] So the entity or the component who are initiating our method execution, we can refer them as a caller.

LECTURE: Introduction to method signature
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss a very important topic which is method signature.
[00:06] Every Java method is going to have a method signature.
[00:09] And this method signature is very helpful in the concepts of method overloading and overriding that
[00:16] we are going to discuss in the coming sections.
[00:18] So what is a method signature?
[00:20] Each method is going to have a signature.
[00:23] This signature is going to help to uniquely identify a method within a specific context or within a
[00:31] specific class.
[00:32] So how the method signature is calculated.
[00:34] The method signature is composed of four important elements.
[00:39] What is the name of the method?
[00:41] What are the types of input parameters?
[00:43] What are the number of input parameters and the order of the parameters?
[00:48] Using these four elements, only a method signature is going to be calculated by your Java compiler.
[00:55] Apart from these four elements, we also have other elements like modifier, return types, parameter
[01:01] names and Throws class as part of the method syntax.
[01:05] But these are not going to be part of the signature of the method.
[01:09] Regardless of which modifier you have mentioned,
[01:11] what is the return type of the method,
[01:13] what are the parameter names that you have discussed, and what is the type of Throws class that you
[01:17] have used?

LECTURE: Constructor chaining in Java
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss the concept of constructor chaining.
[00:05] So what is a constructor chaining.
[00:07] It is a technique that is used inside the object oriented programming to invoke one constructor from
[00:14] another constructor, which is present in the same class.
[00:17] Like, you know, inside the same Java class
[00:20] we can write any number of constructors which accept different types of input parameters.
[00:26] We call that concept as constructor overloading.
[00:28] So when we have multiple constructors defined inside a Java class, it is perfectly possible to invoke
[00:35] one constructor from another constructor.
[00:37] So this concept or this technique, we call it as constructor chaining.
[00:42] For example, if you take the same Employee Java class that we have as of now, we have two constructors
[00:47] inside this Java class, one constructor, which is similar to default constructor.
[00:52] It is not going to accept any input parameters, whereas the other constructor that we have, it is
[00:58] going to accept for input parameters like firstName, lastName, age and gender.
[01:03] So here we have two constructors, and I want to invoke the parameter constructor from my default constructor,
[01:10] or from the constructor where I'm not accepting any parameters. I want to give a chance for you
[01:15] think about it for a second and imagine what should be the solution for this.
[01:20] What is the syntax that we need to follow when we want to invoke a constructor from another constructor?
[01:26] As a new Java developer or a naive developer, you might be thinking like to invoke
[01:32] like you can see here from the first constructor, we are going to invoke the second constructor
[01:37] and in the same process we are going to provide the values like John, Doe, 30, and M.
[01:42] But this is not going to work and you are going to get a compilation error.
[01:47] Do you want to see this in demo?

LECTURE: Static Initialization Block in Java class - Part 1
----------------------------------------

[00:00] From this slide we can see a Java class can contain below components like fields, methods, constructors,
[00:08] instance initializers and static initializers.
[00:11] As of now, we discussed everything except static initializers.
[00:15] Let's try to discuss what are the static initializers and what is the purpose of them.
[00:20] So what is a static initialization block?
[00:22] In Java, a static initialization block is a block of code that is going to be associated with a class,
[00:29] rather than the instances or the objects of the class.
[00:32] Whatever code that we are going to write inside the static initialization block, it is going to be
[00:37] loaded by the JVM.
[00:38] When we try to execute the class for the first time, the primary purpose of the static initialization block
[00:44] is to initialize any static variables of a class.
[00:48] So how to define the static initialization block?
[00:50] It is going to be very simple.
[00:52] First we need to mention the static keyword followed by opening and closing curly braces.
[00:57] They should not be any name to your static initialization block.
[01:01] And this block we need to create outside of the method and constructors, but inside the Java class.
[01:06] So this is one of the sample reference that you can refer.
[01:09] So there is a class with the name Car.
[01:11] And inside this I have a static variable which I just declared.
[01:16] The static variable name is numberOfEngines.
[01:18] This static variable I want to initialize when I try to execute my class.
[01:23] So how to achieve this with the help of static initialization block, you can see I have defined a static
[01:29] initialization block here and inside the body of this block, I am trying to initialize the
[01:34] numberOfEngines to a value called 1.
[01:36] So whatever code that we mentioned inside the static initialization block, it is only going to be executed
[01:43] when the class is loaded into the memory of the JVM, which means it is only going to be executed only
[01:49] once, no matter how many objects or instances of the classes are going to be created, similar to
[01:55] instance initialization block
[01:57] the static initialization block also is not going to have any return statement.
[02:02] This static initialization block is very useful in the scenarios where you want to perform one time initialization
[02:09] of the static variables, or when the initialization logic is more complex and cannot be accommodated
[02:15] with a single line, which means I have some complex logic to calculate the value of a static variable,
[02:21] which I cannot achieve with the single line, like here I have a single line like static byte
[02:26] numberOfEngines.
[02:27] If I want to assign a simple value, I can directly mention here is equal to and what is a value.
[02:32] But in some scenarios, to calculate that initialized value, we need to execute a lot of code.
[02:37] In such scenarios, we can move all such complex initialization logic of the static variable into the
[02:44] static initialization block.
[02:45] If needed
[02:46] you can have multiple static initialization blocks within a class, and all of them are going to be executed
[02:52] in the order in which they appear in the class definition.
[02:55] Whatever code that we are going to write inside the static initialization block is going to be executed
[03:02] before your main() method.
[03:04] So inside Java, we know whenever we want to start or whenever we want to execute a Java program, we
[03:09] use the main() method.
[03:10] So the code inside the static block is going to be executed before the main() method itself, because
[03:16] the code inside this block is going to be invoked by the JVM when it tries to load the Java class.
[03:23] Some interviewers, they can ask a tricky question for you.
[03:26] Can I execute a code before the main() method?
[03:29] So that is perfectly possible.
[03:31] You can do that with the help of static initialization block.
[03:34] I'm also going to show you this in the demo.
[03:36] Now very quickly let's see the difference between a static initialization block and the normal instance
[03:42] initializer block.
[03:44] The very first difference is very simple.
[03:46] The static block is going to have the static keyword.
[03:49] Using the static keyword only, we can difference whether a given block is a static initializer block
[03:54] or the normal instance initializer block.
[03:57] Moving on to the next difference, the static blocks are going to be executed during the class loading,
[04:03] whereas the instance block is going to be executed during the every object creation or every object
[04:10] instantiation.
[04:11] The third difference that we have here is inside the static initialization block, we can refer only
[04:16] the static variables, whereas inside the instance block we can refer both static and non static variables.
[04:23] And the next difference that we have here is in terms of usage of ' this ' keyword inside the static block,
[04:29] we cannot use the this keyword, because this keyword will come into the picture only in the scenarios
[04:35] of object creation or objects
[04:37] related code.
[04:38] Since static block is specific to the class, we cannot use the this keyword, whereas inside the instance
[04:44] block we can use the this keyword without any issues.
[04:48] The last difference that we have here is,
[04:50] this is very important.
[04:52] The static block is only going to be executed only once during the lifetime of a Java program
[04:59] and the
[05:00] execution is going to be during the class loading into the memory and just before the execution of the
[05:06] main() method, whereas instance block is going to be executed each and every time you are trying to create
[05:13] an object.
[05:14] So these are the major differences that I want you to be aware.
[05:18] Please have them handy.
[05:20] I hope you are clear about what is the purpose of static initializer block.
[05:25] In the next lecture, let's try to create this block inside one of the Java class and see this block
[05:30] in action.
[05:31] Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture bye.

[15:47] Why I'm showing this right now because the method invocations inside Java, they follow the stack data
[15:55] structure.
[15:55] So how the stack data structure works by using a principle called LAST IN FIRST OUT (LIFO). In short form
[16:03] we can also call it as leaf or LIFO.
[16:06] That means inside a stack, whatever last element came into the picture, that is the first element
[16:13] which is going to be removed from the stack.
[16:16] So here you can see there are good amount of plates.
[16:18] So what is the last plate that joined the stack,
[16:21] the top plate.
[16:22] So if you want to remove a plate first you need to remove the last plate that came into the stack.
[16:28] So that's why we call the design principle of stack as last in first out.
[16:33] The same principle is followed inside the method invocations as well.
[16:38] Whatever is the latest method that you invoke that will be at the top of the method stack?
[16:43] I can also show you that in the demo once.
[16:46] So here, let me keep a breakpoint inside the method4().
[16:49] Because this is the last method, we are going to invoke and remove this breakpoint inside the main()

[16:59] So what is the top method that we have?
[17:02] The method that which entered at the end.
[17:05] So method4() came at the end,
[17:07] that's why it is a top element inside the stack that is maintained by the JVM.
[17:12] So if you want to execute method3(), first you need to complete the method4() execution, because
[17:18] method3() is dependent on the method4().
[17:21] If I click on this step out, then the method4() execution will be completed.
[17:25] That means the top element at the stack will be removed, and you can see right now the top element

LECTURE: Introduction to null in Java
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Null has a very important significance inside Java,
[00:04] let's try to understand the same inside this lecture.
[00:07] So what is a null, in Java
[00:09] null is a reserved keyword that denotes a variable or a attribute, but does not reference to any object,
[00:17] which means you only declared a variable by providing a reference data type, but you have not created
[00:23] an object or you have not assigned any object to that variable.
[00:27] In such scenarios, we can say that variable or attribute is going to hold the null value.
[00:33] So null indicates an absence of an instance or an object associated with a given variable or field.
[00:41] This might be very confusing.
[00:42] Let me give you an example.
[00:44] Here you can see I'm trying to create two variables or attributes or Java fields by using the reference
[00:51] data types.
[00:52] So what are the reference data types I'm trying to use here String and Employee.
[00:56] How I'm saying these are reference data types because String and Employee they both are Java classes.
[01:03] Whenever I try to assign these reference data types to a given variable or attribute or Java field,
[01:10] then there is a chance that variable is going to hold the null value.
[01:14] So when the null value is going to be hold by the variable, if you don't initialize the object or
[01:19] if you don't assign the object to the given variable.
[01:22] Here you can see the very first one,
[01:24] I'm simply declaring my String variable, and I'm trying to assign a value called null, which means
[01:30] my String is going to hold the null value which I have assigned specifically.
[01:35] The same can happen even with the second line of statement, where I'm trying to declare only the variable
[01:41] name but not initializing.
[01:42] I just mentioned what is the data type and what is the variable name which is Employee object.
[01:47] In this scenario, also, the Employee object is going to hold the null value.
[01:52] Usually inside the Java developers, they are going to declare the variables at the starting of the
[01:57] method later on inside the method, by using the same variables, they're going to create an object,
[02:04] or they're going to assign an object to these variables.
[02:07] As we try to create more and more examples inside this course, then it is going to make more sense
[02:12] to you.
[02:13] One important point that we need to aware in terms of null keyword is whenever a null value is assigned
[02:20] to a variable or a attribute, there is a good chance that NullPointerException may happen at runtime
[02:27] if you try to access the fields with the help of that object reference.
[02:31] So here you can see I have an object reference with the name Employee object.
[02:35] I know using the e\Employee object I can access the instance fields like firstName, lastName, age
[02:41] and gender.
[02:41] So if I try to do that with this Employee object which is going to hold the null value, since null
[02:46] indicates absence of an instance or object, I'm going to get an error or RuntimeException which is
[02:54] NullPointerException.
[02:55] To avoid this, always developers, they are going to do a null check before they try to access
[03:00] the fields or before they try to invoke the methods with the help of object references, we are going
[03:06] to talk more about what is an exception, how to avoid that, and what are NullPointerExceptions in
[03:11] the coming sections.
[03:12] For now, I just wanted to give this quick information.
[03:15] So whatever we are talking right now regarding null keywords, this is only applicable for the reference

LECTURE: Checking if a String is empty
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Sometimes in the business logic that you are trying to write with the help of Java programming language,

[00:15] Otherwise you want to execute other set of business logic.
[00:19] To handle these kind of situations, you need to know how to check if a given String object holds empty
[00:26] data or not.

[00:34] Let's try to explore all these three options.
[00:37] The very first option is with the help of isEmpty() method.
[00:41] Inside String there is a non-static method or there is a instance method.

[00:52] If your String object holds empty data, this is empty.
[00:56] Method is going to return a boolean value as an output, and the boolean value is going to hold true
[01:02] value if the String is empty
[01:05] otherwise you're going to get false as an output.
[01:08] Before I try to reveal the second approach, I want to give you a hint.
[01:11] We already discussed about the length() method with the help of length() method
[01:16] can we identify if a given String is empty or not?

[01:25] String does not hold any character, then the length value is going to be zero.

LECTURE: Searching for a value in String
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Searching for a given value inside String is a most common scenario in real projects.
[00:07] For example, think like I have a sentence stored inside a String object.
[00:12] The sentence goes like this
[00:14] my name is Madan.
[00:16] If I want to search this String, if it contains my name which is Madan, I need to search for it.
[00:22] If the name Madan available inside the given String, then it is a match
[00:26] otherwise it is not a match.
[00:28] So how to perform this kind of searching in a given String data, there are multiple approaches to search
[00:35] a given String.
[00:37] The very first approach is with the help of indexOf() method.
[00:40] indexOf() is a instance method or a non-static method, which we can invoke with the help of
[00:46] String object.
[00:47] To this indexOf() method, you need to pass what you are trying to search and to whatever input data
[00:53] that you have provided to this indexOf() method is going to be searched inside the original String that
[01:00] you have provided, and if there is a match for your given input data, then this indexOf() method is
[01:07] going to return the index number at the position where the given word or given data is available inside
[01:16] the original String.
[01:17] Here you can see I have an example where inside the original String I stored that data, which is Hello,

LECTURE: Converting String to primitive data type values - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Few lectures back, we discuss on how to convert a primitive data into an String value.
[00:07] Do you remember this?
[00:08] I hope you remember this concept with the help of the valueOf() method, which is available inside the
[00:14] String, we can convert any primitive data into an string representation.
[00:20] For example, here I have an int value 42.
[00:23] If I give this 42 as an input to the valueOf()method, which is a static method inside String, I am
[00:30] going to get an string representation of that 42.
[00:33] So what is the string representation of 42?
[00:36] A 42 with a double quotes value is a string representation.
[00:39] So this is a scenario where we want to convert a primitive data type into a String object.
[00:45] Sometimes we may want to convert a String object into a corresponding primitive data type.
[00:51] So let's try to understand how to achieve the same.
[00:54] The process of converting a String data into a primitive data type.
[00:58] We call that process as parsing.
[01:01] Parsing involves converting a string representation of a value into its corresponding primitive data
[01:07] type.
[01:07] So how to perform this parsing operation?
[01:10] I may have an int value in the format of String, but I want to convert that into a normal into primitive
[01:17] value.
[01:17] So for this kind of parsing scenarios we need to use a wrapper classes.
[01:22] Do you remember long back I told you that every primitive data type it has a corresponding wrapper class.
[01:29] For example, for into primitive data type, we have a wrapper class with the name Integer.
[01:34] Inside this Integer wrapper class, we have a static method which is parseInt().
[01:40] This parseInt() method is going to accept a String object as an input, and inside this String object,
[01:47] we need to make sure we are providing only the int values like numeric values.
[01:52] If you try to be oversmart and try to provide some alphanumeric values to this parseInt() method, it
[01:59] is going to throw an NumberFormatException.
[02:01] But if you give a proper int value using a String object, this pass int is going to give you an int
[02:08] value as an output.
[02:10] That's why here you can see for the parseInt() method, I'm trying to pass the string number as an input,
[02:16] and the return type that I'm receiving from this method is of type int primitive data type.
[02:21] Very similarly, if you are trying to convert a String object which has a double value into the double
[02:26] primitive data type, then you need to use a corresponding wrapper class which is Double.
[02:32] Inside the Double wrapper class, we have a method which is parseDouble(). To this parseDouble(),
[02:38] if you give a String object, it is going to convert your double number from string to primitive data
[02:44] type.
[02:44] For the float, it is going to be very similar.
[02:47] The wrapper class is going to be Float, and inside this wrapper class we have a method which is pass
[02:53] float that we need to invoke.
[02:54] After the float, we can see the example of Long.
[02:58] If you want to convert a Long string value into a primitive long value, you can use a wrapper class
[03:04] long.
[03:05] And inside this Long class we have a parseLong() method which we need to invoke, and this parseLong() method
[03:11] is going to convert your string data into a long primitive data type.
[03:16] In case if you are looking to convert your boolean string value into the boolean primitive data type
[03:22] value, then Boolean has a wrapper class with the name boolean where b is capital.
[03:27] Inside this Boolean wrapper class, we have a method which is parseBoolean().
[03:32] To this method, you need to pass your string representation of your boolean value.
[03:37] So here I'm trying to pass the true.
[03:39] So the output is going to be the true which is in the form of Boolean data type.
[03:44] If you try to be smart and if you're trying to send some values other than true and false, you're always
[03:50] going to get the output as false from this method.
[03:54] For example, I can pass my name as an input to this parseBoolean().
[03:58] If I pass my name as an input, then obviously that will be converted into an false value.
[04:05] So anything other than true and false always going to be converted into a false.
[04:10] Otherwise, if you are going to send the true value, you're going to get the true as an output.
[04:15] And similarly, if you send the false as an input, you are going to get the false as an output for
[04:19] the number scenarios like int, long, float, and double.
[04:23] If you try to send some invalid values, like maybe you're trying to send a alpha value.
[04:29] In such scenarios like we discussed, we're always going to get number format exception.
[04:34] So using the wrapper classes and invoking the static methods like parseBoolean(), parseLong(), parseInt()
[04:40] int parseFloat(), parseDouble().
[04:42] So this is one approach
[04:44] there is also another approach which you can achieve with the help of constructor of your wrapper classes.
[04:50] So here you can see I'm trying to create an object of wrapper class Integer.
[04:55] During the same process I can pass the String object as an
[04:59] input to the constructor.
[05:01] And with that, I'm going to get an object of Integer object.
[05:05] From this Integer object, we can fetch the actual valueOf() int, but this approach is deprecated from
[05:13] the Java 9.
[05:14] So what is the meaning of deprecated, Java team
[05:16] regularly they are going to deprecate some methods, some functionalities, some features.
[05:22] The purpose of deprecate is,
[05:24] in future versions they may remove these options.
[05:27] So here you may have a question like why Java team deprecate some features or some methods.
[05:33] The answer is very simple due to some performance issues are some security concerns,
[05:38] the reason can be anything Java team.
[05:40] Whenever they found some issues, they're going to make the features or the methods or classes deprecated.
[05:47] So when you try to use this deprecated approach inside our projects, it is considered as a bad practice.
[05:53] That's why always don't use that deprecated approaches.
[05:57] The reason why I'm sharing this information is you may work in an project where they are using Java 8,
[06:02] since inside the Java 8 this is not deprecated.
[06:05] You don't know that, but from Java 9 this method or this approach is deprecated.
[06:11] So all of a sudden a valid code inside the Java 8 is going to become invalid from the future versions
[06:19] like Java 9.
[06:19] So that's why regardless of which version you are using, please don't use this approach.
[06:25] As of now, we discussed the parsing process for the primitive data types like int, float, double

[07:07] So this is the very first approach.
[07:09] And the second approach is using your String object

LECTURE: Deep dive on switch case statement - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, we discuss on how to write the conditional Java statements with the help of if statements.
[00:07] On the very similar lines
[00:08] we can also use switch case statements to write conditional statements inside Java.
[00:15] So there are two approaches for the developers.
[00:17] One is with the help of if statements and the other one is with the help of switch case statement.
[00:23] Here you may have a question, which is why we have two different approaches inside Java and when to
[00:29] use which approach.
[00:30] To explain you about the same.
[00:32] First, let me give you a problem.
[00:34] Think like there is a supermarket and inside this supermarket they are going to sell lot
[00:39] many fruits like banana, apple, grapes, pineapple, mango.
[00:43] So for each of the fruit the price is going to be different.
[00:47] So the owner of the supermarket, he asks you to develop a Java logic to determine what is the price
[00:54] that he has to charge to the customer based upon the fruit selected by the customer.
[00:59] To solve this problem,
[01:01] if you go with the if statement approach, your logic is going to look like this.
[01:05] Like first I'm going to check if the fruit name is equal to banana
[01:09] if yes, I'm going to print a statement,
[01:11] $1 is charged and post that I can write else if statements to check apple, to check grapes to check
[01:19] pineapple and to check mango.
[01:22] And at last I can have an else statement if my fruit name is not equal to any of the valid fruit names,
[01:28] I'm going to print a statement which is pick a valid fruit with the help of else statement.
[01:34] This may look very good for you, but if you closely observe this Java program that we built with the
[01:39] help of if statements, we are trying to evaluate the condition at multiple places at each if block
[01:47] and else if block,
[01:48] I'm trying to check whether my fruit name is equal to so and so value.
[01:52] So the condition is getting evaluated multiple times.
[01:55] On top of that, my code also is looking very lengthy and clumsy.
[02:00] So as the conditions that you have to evaluate is going to increase, the amount of code that you are
[02:07] going to write is also going to be increased.
[02:09] On top of that, you need to evaluate the condition for each and every if and else if blocks.
[02:16] So to overcome this challenge we have switch case statement inside Java.
[02:21] So whenever you have these kind of scenarios where you have to evaluate lot many conditions, in such
[02:27] cases you can use more efficient approach which is switch case statement.
[02:34] I hope you are clear when to use switch case statement. As a next ste,
[02:38] let's try to understand the syntax of the switch case statement.
[02:42] The syntax of the switch case statement is going to be very simple.
[02:46] Like you can see
[02:47] first we need to start the switch statement with the help of switch keyword.
[02:51] And after that inside the parentheses you need to write an Java expression, which is going to be evaluated
[02:57] only once based upon the outcome from the expression
[03:00] one of the case that we have defined inside the switch block is going to be executed.
[03:06] You can see I have so many case statements.
[03:09] With the help of case, I have defined a label1, label2, label3.
[03:13] So if my expression is evaluated to a value which is equal to label1, then whatever statements I
[03:21] have written under this case is going to be evaluated.
[03:24] Similarly
[03:25] the same is going to happen for label2 and label3.
[03:28] If my Java expression is not evaluated to any of the label values in such scenarios, the default block
[03:36] is going to be executed.
[03:38] So under default I can write some Java statements.
[03:41] And if you closely observe the syntax, we also have a break keyword used inside each of the case,
[03:48] including the default.
[03:49] The purpose of the break is whenever your expression is evaluated to one of the label,
[03:55] whatever Java statements that you have under that label case are going to be executed.
[04:00] Once these execution of this statements is completed, you want to break the flow and come out of this
[04:07] switch expression.
[04:08] If you don't have this break, then your switch case is going to execute the next case labels as well.
[04:14] So this break is completely optional.
[04:17] If you don't mention this break keyword inside all your case labels and default block, then in such
[04:23] scenarios you may get an unexpected results.
[04:27] For example, think like this expression is evaluated to a label2.
[04:31] In this scenario, you might be expecting only the case label2 to be executed, but in the scenario
[04:38] where you are not mentioning the break, all the next label cases and the default block also is going
[04:44] to be executed.
[04:45] So as soon as this case label2 is executed, since there won't be any break, the execution will
[04:50] jump to the label3.
[04:52] And if the label3 also does not have break statement, it will go to the last block which is default
[04:57] block.
[04:58] So to avoid this kind of behavior
[05:00] always make sure you are mentioning the break keyword inside each of your cases, including the default
[05:08] one.
[05:08] So we have an expression after the switch keyword.
[05:11] So the value that is going to be derived from this expression has to be of type byte, short, char, int, enum
[05:21] or String.
[05:22] Remaining data types are not allowed.
[05:24] For example, the boolean is missing from this list and float, double, long
[05:30] all these values are missing from this list.
[05:32] That means you cannot write an Java expression, which is going to result as a boolean, or a float,
[05:39] or a double, or a long,
[05:41] whenever you are using the switch case statement.
[05:44] On top of that, one more important point that you need to take care is whatever label1, label2
[05:51] values that you are going to define against each of the case.
[05:54] They have to be compile time constant expressions.
[05:58] You can't define a variable or an expression against these labels like label1, label2 and label3.
[06:04] .
[06:05] I'm going to show you all these in demo.
[06:07] Then it is going to make more sense to you.
[06:09] So whenever you are trying to build a switch case statement, by following this syntax, all these steps
[06:14] are going to be executed.
[06:16] First
[06:16] the Java expression is going to be evaluated and based upon the value derived, one of the case label
[06:23] will be selected and all the statements inside the case label block will be executed by the switch statement.
[06:30] So this way with the help of switch case statement
[06:33] also, we're able to control the execution of the Java statements.
[06:36] Let me show you an example on how to write the switch case statement

[07:18] Post that we have a break statement.
[07:20] You can see this time the code is looking very neat and we are not evaluating the condition at the multiple
[07:27] places.
[07:27] We are simply evaluating that Java expression only once and based upon the value from the Java expression,
[07:35] we are going to execute one of the case.
[07:38] I hope you are clear.
[07:39] Now let me share more important details about the switch case statement.
[07:43] Like I said before, whenever you are trying to use the switch case statement, please make sure that
[07:48] your expression is not going to evaluate a value of type boolean, long, float, and double.
[07:56] Even if you try to pass a variable of type boolean, long, float and double to your switch statement,
[08:03] you are going to get an compilation error.
[08:05] And the second point that I want to highlight here is the break statement, like we discussed is used
[08:11] to exit the switch statement once the corresponding code segment is executed.
[08:17] Otherwise all the following cases will be executed.
[08:21] That's why always make sure you are mentioning the break statement inside your switch case statement.
[08:28] If you closely look at this switch case statement, the last case that we have is default.
[08:33] So default also has a break statement.
[08:35] And here you may have a question which is anywhere below the default
[08:40] we don't have any other cases to be executed with that assumption
[08:44] you might be thinking why should we mention break statement inside the default?
[08:48] I agree with you.
[08:49] Technically the final break is not required because the flow anywhere falls out of the switch statement,
[08:57] but using a break statement is strongly recommended so that in future, if any of the other developer

[09:24] As of now, you can see inside my switch case statement, I'm using an expression which which is going

[00:47] expression or a switch case statement.
[00:50] In the case of switch case statement, after the case label, we are supposed to mention colon, whereas
[00:57] inside the switch expression we can mention the arrow symbol.

[01:07] where you want to execute a common logic for different case labels, you can simply mention all those
[01:14] labels by using comma separator.

[01:32] Apart from these improvements, whenever you are trying to use a switch expression, you don't have

[07:29] So let's try to understand those.
[07:31] The very first best practice that you need to follow is whenever you are trying to declare local variables,
[07:36] please try to declare them with the narrowest scope possible.
[07:40] That means if you need a variable within the if block, declare it only within the if block.
[07:47] Don't try to declare the local variable outside of your if block within the method, because with that,
[07:53] you are going to increase the scope of your local variable from if block to the method.
[07:59] So this best practice is going to help you in preventing the naming conflicts, and reduces the risk
[08:06] of the accidental modification of the variable values.
[08:10] And the next best practice is, try to give some meaningful variable names for your local variables,
[08:16] so that your code can be easily understand by other developers.
[08:21] Moving on to the next best practice, always make sure to initialize the variables whenever you are
[08:27] trying to declare them.
[08:28] For primitive data types, you don't have to initialize anything because all the primitive data types,
[08:33] they are going to have a default value.
[08:36] Whereas if you are trying to declare a Person object or a String object, don't try to leave them by
[08:42] just declaring them.
[08:44] At least try to initialize them with a null value so that it gives an indication to the other developers
[08:50] that so and so variable object is going to hold a null value, and they need to be very careful while
[08:56] trying to access it, since it may result into NullPointerException.
[09:00] If they don't perform the null check the next standard is,
[09:03] always make sure you are declaring only one variable per line.
[09:08] So Java allows you to define any number of variables in a single line.
[09:12] It's not a good practice because for other developers it is going to be super tough to read your code.
[09:18] So to make your code more readable and maintainable, always try to declare one variable per line moving
[09:25] on to the next best practice, which is avoid declaring unnecessary variables.
[09:31] If you don't need a variable inside your business logic, then don't declare it so
[09:35] this is the simple thumb rule that you need to follow.
[09:38] Otherwise you will have so many unused or unnecessary variables inside your business logic, which will
[09:43] make your code complex to understand and clumsy.
[09:47] And the last, best practice that we have is keep a variable declarations close to their first use.
[09:53] For example, think like your method has 1000 lines of Java code and you are going to use a

[10:31] number two.

LECTURE: Rules & standards to name a package
----------------------------------------

[00:00] While we are trying to give a name to a Java package, we need to follow certain standards along with
[00:07] rules and regulations.
[00:08] Inside this lecture, let's try to understand what are those.
[00:11] Like I said before, there is a very good chance that two different developers from two different organizations
[00:18] are from two different teams.
[00:19] They may end up choosing the same name for a Java class or an interface.
[00:24] So to avoid name conflicts inside a Java project, we have packages and inside two different packages

LECTURE: Introduction to access modifiers
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, whenever we are trying to create a Java class or a Java method or a Java field, in all
[00:06] these scenarios we are using the public access modifier.
[00:11] But apart from public access modifiers, there are other access modifiers also available inside Java.
[00:17] Since these access modifiers are tightly coupled with the concept of packages, I have not discussed
[00:23] about them as of now.
[00:25] But now since we know everything about the packages, it is the right time to discuss about the access
[00:31] modifiers in Java.
[00:32] So what is our purpose of access modifiers in Java?
[00:35] With the help of these access modifiers, we can specify what is the visibility of our Classes,
[00:42] Methods and variables or fields, which means I can control who can access my class or who can access
[00:50] my methods and variables.
[00:52] In Java there are four access modifier.
[00:54] The very first access modifier that we have is public.
[00:58] We are using these public access modifier a lot.
[01:01] as of now.
[01:02] Whenever we are using these modifier as part of the class definition or method definition or variable
[01:08] declaration.
[01:09] In those scenarios we are letting to access our class, our method, our variable from anywhere.
[01:16] When I say anywhere within the class or outside the class, or from any other class which is present
[01:22] inside another package. There are no restrictions
[01:25] anyone can access our class, method
[01:28] or variable. The next access modifier that we have is private.
[01:31] So this is completely opposite of public.
[01:34] Whenever we are defining a private access modifier for a class, method or a variable, it can only
[01:40] be accessed within the same class where it is declared.
[01:44] Here you may have a question which is how can I access a class within a class for that
[01:49] the answer is very simple.
[01:50] Java allows you to declare inner classes as part of a outer class.
[01:55] That means your Java class can contain other Java classes.
[01:58] When you make your inner class as an private class, that class can be only be accessed within the same
[02:06] class, whereas for methods and variables, it should be pretty clear for you.
[02:10] If you define a private method or a private variable, the method or variable can only be accessed within
[02:17] the same class.
[02:17] So understanding public and private should be pretty simple.
[02:21] The third access modifier that we have is protected, when we define a class, our method or variable
[02:27] as protected.
[02:28] In such scenario, the class
[02:30] or method
[02:31] or variable can only be accessed by the classes in the same package, and subclasses which are present
[02:39] inside or outside of the same package.
[02:41] So what is a subclass?
[02:43] Subclass is a concept that we are going to discuss as part of the inheritance concept.
[02:48] Using the inheritance concept, a Java class can inherit another Java class.
[02:53] That means a Java class can act as a parent to the child Java class.
[02:58] In this kind of scenarios, the child class we can call it as subclass.
[03:02] So more details about subclasses inheritance we are going to discuss in the coming sections.
[03:07] For now
[03:07] please note that when we define a access modifier protected, all the classes in the same package can
[03:14] access our class, method or variable.
[03:17] But if one of the class which is outside of the package is trying to access them, they will be able
[03:23] to access only if the class is a subclass of the given class where we have defined the protected access
[03:29] modifier.
[03:29] I know it may be confusing to you to understand about protected.
[03:34] Don't worry, when we discuss about inheritance it is going to be super clear for you.
[03:38] For now, please focus on that definition.
[03:40] Next, moving on to the last access modifier which is default.
[03:44] If you are not mentioning any access modifier for your class, method or variable, then behind the
[03:51] scenes Java is going to consider that default access modifier.
[03:55] Whenever we are using the default access modifier, it is going to provide package private access that
[04:02] means any class, method or variable which are using default access modifier
[04:08] they can only be accessed within the same package, but not from the outside of the package.
[04:14] I hope you are clear with these definitions.
[04:16] Always make sure you are using the access modifiers to control the access to your classes, methods
[04:23] and variables.
[04:24] You should not build a business logic by using completely public access modifier or private or protected
[04:31] or default.
[04:32] You should use a mix of these modifiers based upon your business requirements.
[04:37] If there is a method which is going to be accessed to only within the same class, then in such scenarios
[04:43] it is always makes sense to make that method as private instead of public.
[04:48] Why do you want to unnecessarily expose your method to the other classes or other packages?
[04:53] So these kind of restrictions you can achieve with the help of access modifiers in Java.
[05:00] Let me show you a very quick example here.

[05:24] That means the last variable which is defaultVar, it is going to have the access modifier default

[06:09] or variable declaration.
[06:11] Inside these examples, like you can see, since publicVar and publicMethod has a access modifier
[06:17] public, they can be accessed from anywhere inside your project, even from other packages, whereas

LECTURE: is-a & has-a relationships in Java
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside Java are in any object oriented programming language we can use is-a relationship or has-a relationship
[00:09] to represent our established relationship between different classes. Inside your Java interviews or
[00:16] inside your Java related exams.
[00:18] Definitely
[00:19] sometimes you may hear questions about what is a , is-a relationship or has-a relationship in Java.
[00:26] So let's try to understand what are those. Using is-a relationship we can express Inheritance relationship
[00:34] between two classes.
[00:35] So whenever we use extends keyword that means we are establishing Inheritance relationship between a
[00:42] superclass and a subclass.
[00:44] For example, here I have a superclass with the name Animal, and I also have a subclass that is extending
[00:51] the Animal superclass, and the subclass name is Dog.
[00:54] So both of these Dog and Animal, they have a relationship which is established with the help of inheritance
[01:01] concept.
[01:02] So this kind of relationship that is established with the help of inheritance, in other words we can
[01:08] call it as is-a relationship.
[01:10] So how this is an is-a relationship.
[01:12] So let's try to understand the same.
[01:14] So if someone asks you what is a Dog, you will say Dog is a animal.
[01:20] Very similarly, we can also say SpiderMan is a Person, Car is a Vehicle, Orange is a Fruit.
[01:27] So this way using is-a relationship, we can always express our establish Inheritance relationship between
[01:36] two classes.
[01:37] If you can't build a sentence like Dog is-a Animal, you should not be establishing the Inheritance.
[01:43] It is not going to make sense.
[01:45] For example, if I say SpiderMan is-a Vehicle, do you think it is going to make any sense?
[01:51] off course not.
[01:52] That's why in this kind of scenarios, I should not try to establish the Inheritance between Vehicle
[01:58] and SpiderMan.
[01:59] Though your compiler is not going to stop anything around this, but it is a best practice to make sure
[02:05] that you are establishing the Inheritance only when a is-a relationship is established between different
[02:12] classes.
[02:12] I hope you are clear.
[02:13] What is an is-a relationship?
[02:15] Now let's try to understand what is a has-a relationship.
[02:19] Has a relationship is used to indicate that a given class has a certain property or object of another
[02:27] class.
[02:27] For example, here I have a class with the name Car, and inside this Car I can create any number of
[02:34] instance variable, and these instance variables can belong to another classes as well.
[02:40] For example, you can see I have an instance variable created inside my Car class,
[02:45] what is the instance variable?
[02:47] It is engine of data type Engine class.
[02:50] So here I have an Engine class, using the same Engine class
[02:54] I'm trying to create an instance variable inside my Car class.
[02:59] That means my Car class is holding an a property of another class.
[03:05] So this kind of relationship we can call it as has-a relationship.
[03:10] So here there is no inheritance involved.
[03:13] But my given class has an embedded property or a variable representing another class.
[03:20] So since a Car is going to have an engine in real world also, it is going to make a perfect sense to
[03:27] create an engine related embedded variable inside my car
[03:32] and with that we are going to establish an has-a relationship between Car and Engine.
[03:38] In other words we can also call this has-a relationship as aggregation or composition.
[03:45] So please make a note of this very important point.
[03:48] So people may ask you in interviews in a different style.
[03:52] So they may ask you what is an aggregation or a composition in Java.
[03:57] In such scenarios, you should explain about the has-a relationship that we are discussing right now.
[04:03] So with the help of is-a relationship, we can always implement inheritance
[04:08] and with inheritance we are encouraging lot of code reusability, whereas with the help of has-a relationship,
[04:16] we are going to represent an object which is a composition or aggregation of many other objects.

LECTURE: What a subclass inherits from its superclass
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Based upon our discussions in the previous lecture.
[00:03] Now, you should be pretty clear about the basics of the inheritance.
[00:08] So what is the purpose of inheritance?
[00:10] Whenever we implement inheritance, a subclass can inherit Java fields and Java method from its superclass.
[00:18] But usually inside a superclass we can write lot of other types of members as well. Like static fields,
[00:25] static methods, instance methods, instance variables, constructors.
[00:30] So there'll be different kinds of members, usually inside a Java class.
[00:34] And we should not be under the assumption everything inside the superclass is going to be inherited
[00:40] by the subclass.
[00:41] So that's not going to be the case.
[00:43] There are certain limitations, our rules and regulations that you need to be aware.
[00:48] So let's try to understand what are those inside this lecture.
[00:51] Like I said before, it is important to note that a class does not automatically acquire or inherit
[00:58] everything from its superclass class.
[01:00] It is going to selectively inherit Non-private members from the superclass.
[01:06] That means the members of the class that are declared with the public, default, and protected, they are
[01:13] going to be passed down or inherited to the subclass, whereas private members they are going to be
[01:20] remain confined within the superclass, and they are not going to be accessible to the subclass.
[01:26] I'm going to talk in detail how access modifiers are going to influence the inheritance process in few
[01:32] minutes.
[01:33] But before that, let's try to understand few general rules and regulations and thumb rules that we
[01:39] need to be aware around inheritance.
[01:42] The very first rule is the constructors and the initializers that we are going to write inside a superclass.
[01:48] They are not going to be inherited by the subclass.
[01:52] A superclass can have any number of constructors, and it may also have a static initializer or a instance
[01:59] initializer.
[02:00] So since these are not fall under the category of the members within a class, they are not going to
[02:07] participate in the inheritance process.
[02:10] Moving on to the next rule, all the static members that you are going to define inside your superclass,
[02:17] they are going to be inherited by the subclass.
[02:19] When I say static members, what are those?
[02:21] It can be a static field or a static method.
[02:24] So these static methods and static fields, they will be inherited by the subclass without any issues.
[02:32] We're also going to see the demo in few minutes.
[02:34] Apart from static members like static fields and static methods, we can also define instance method
[02:41] and instance variables.
[02:42] We know that these instance methods and instance variables
[02:46] they are also going to be participate in the inheritance process regardless whether a method is static
[02:51] or non static, whether a field is static or non static.
[02:55] So all of them, they are going to participate in the inheritance process.
[02:59] But they are going to be greatly influenced by the access modifiers.
[03:05] For example, if you define a class member with a private access modifier, its accessibility is going
[03:12] to be restricted solely to the class in which it is declared.
[03:16] That means private class members are not going to be passed down to the subclasses, and they are going
[03:22] to be remain exclusive, but the superclass alone. After the private
[03:27] we can also define class members by using the public access modifier.
[03:32] So when we use the public access modifier, all of your class members, they are going to be inherited
[03:39] to the subclass.
[03:40] That means a subclass inherits all public members of its superclass, whether it is a method or a field.
[03:47] If it is a public, the same is going to be inherited by the subclass.
[03:51] On the similar lines, when we define a class member with a package level or a default access modifier,
[03:58] then in this kind of scenarios, if the subclass is present inside the same package, then these default
[04:04] are package level class members
[04:06] they are going to be inherited by the subclass, whereas if your subclass is belongs to a different
[04:12] package compared to the superclass, then in such scenario, the subclass does not going to inherit
[04:18] package level members or default members from its superclass.
[04:23] So to resolve this challenge, we can use protected Access modifier.
[04:28] When we use the protected access modifier, your subclass always going to inherit that class members
[04:35] regardless your subclass present inside the same package of superclass or a different package compared
[04:40] to the superclass.
[04:41] So these are the guidelines or the rules that you need to be aware to understand.
[04:46] What is subclass inherits from its superclass.

LECTURE: Introduction to downcasting & it's demo
----------------------------------------

[00:00] What is downcasting ? downcasting is the exact opposite of upcasting.
[00:06] Inside the upcasting, we are going to assign the object of a subclass to the superclass, but if you
[00:12] try to do the exactly opposite of it, which is assign an object of superclass to the object reference
[00:18] of subclass, then we are going to call it as downcasting.
[00:22] First, let me show you a demo of downcasting.
[00:25] Later on, we can discuss more details about downcasting. For the same here
[00:30] inside my app package, I'm going to create a new Java class with the name DownCastingDemo.
[00:37] Inside this DownCastingDemo.
[00:39] First I'm going to create the main() method inside my main() method
[00:43] first I'm going to create the object reference of superclass which is Animal pose.
[00:48] This Animal object reference I want to create the object of Dog class.
[00:53] So let me create it with the help of new operator and default constructor of Dog class.
[00:59] So now you can see we have a object reference of superclass.
[01:03] And we also have an subclass object.
[01:06] So if you try to type anm = dog.
[01:11] So this is perfectly acceptable inside Java because this is upcasting because we are trying to assign
[01:18] an subclass object to the superclass object reference.
[01:22] But if you try to do the opposite of it, we are going to get a compilation error.
[01:27] So let me type dog = anm.
[01:31] So you can see I'm getting a compilation error because inside Java by default downcasting is not allowed.
[01:39] So to resolve this compilation error we need to tell specifically to the compiler.
[01:44] I'm aware of the fact that I'm trying to downcast, and I'm sure that these Animal object reference
[01:49] is holding the Dog object, so we need to give an assurance to the compiler to resolve this error.
[01:56] So how to give that assurance just before your anm object reference we need to mention parentheses.
[02:03] And inside the parentheses we need to mention the subclass name which is Dog.
[02:07] And with that you can see the downcasting
[02:10] right now it is allowed.
[02:11] So here we are trying to assign a superclass object reference or superclass object data type to a subclass
[02:19] object to reference.
[02:21] So this is called downcasting.
[02:23] So why Java is not allowing this automatically is by default we can't say that every Animal is a Dog.
[02:30] It is going to be invalid because under Animal we may have cat, we may have horse, we may have elephant.
[02:35] So since it is invalid to call every Animal as a dog, your compilation is going to stop you with a
[02:41] compilation error.
[02:42] So you as a developer, you need to give a assurance or confidence to your Java compiler saying that
[02:49] that these anm is holding the object of Dog.
[02:52] So how to give that confident or assurance by mentioning the subclass name within the parentheses just
[02:59] before this name.
[03:00] So the same kind of syntax we also followed for primitive data types casting as well.
[03:05] So with this syntax we are able to manually perform the downcasting.
[03:10] But whenever we are trying to perform the downcasting we need to be very careful.
[03:14] We need to perform the downcasting only if we are 100% sure that these anm is going to hold the object
[03:22] of Dog.
[03:22] Otherwise we are going to get a RuntimeException which is ClassCastException.
[03:28] So let me show you a demo around this.
[03:30] For the same I'm going to first create the object reference of Cat subclass, followed by I'm going
[03:37] to assign the a anm object reference.
[03:40] And with that I'm going to get a compilation error because by default downcasting is not allowed.
[03:45] So to resolve this issue I can simply say Cat within the parentheses and my compilation error is resolved.
[03:53] But if I try to execute this program at runtime, I'm going to get a ClassCastException.
[03:59] I can show you that as well by running my program in a debug mode.
[04:03] You can see I got a ClassCastException saying that inside my anm object reference we are holding the
[04:10] Dog object, but we are trying to assign that to the Cat.

[04:19] That's why we are getting the ClassCastException at line number 16.
[04:25] So that's why always please make sure you are 100% sure that your object reference is holding the actual

LECTURE: Method Overloading - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, we understand what is an method overriding in Java.
[00:05] As a next step, let's try to understand what is method overloading and how we can achieve static polymorphism
[00:12] with the help of method overloading.
[00:14] Inside Java, whenever we want to perform the method overloading, there is no mandatory that you need
[00:19] to implement inheritance even in a normal and independent class
[00:25] also, you can implement method overloading.
[00:27] So first I'm going to show you an example where I'm not following any inheritance post that I'll also
[00:33] show you another example on how to perform the method overloading.
[00:37] When we implemented inheritance between two classes.
[00:41] Coming to that definition of the method overloading, it is a feature in Java that allows a developer
[00:47] to define multiple methods with the same name in the same class.
[00:53] However, the methods must have different parameters list.
[00:58] Though the method names are same, but they are going to hold the different number of parameters or different
[01:04] data types of parameters, or both of them the return type and the access modifier and the Throws class
[01:10] of a method
[01:11] they are not going to play any role in making an method overloaded, and at the same time using different
[01:18] names for the method parameters does not going to make the method overloaded.
[01:23] I have an example class and this class
[01:27] it is not inheriting any superclass.
[01:29] If you closely look at the class body inside this example class, we have three different methods with
[01:36] the same name print and all of these methods
[01:39] they have different parameters as an input.
[01:42] For example, for the first print() method, I'm having the input parameter as int followed by double
[01:49] and at last
[01:50] for the last print() method, we are accepting the String data type as an input parameter.
[01:56] So this is a perfect example of method overloading.
[01:59] Though the name of the three methods is same, but they are having different method input parameters.
[02:06] So in this kind of scenario the Static Binding or compile time binding is going to happen.
[02:13] And that's why whenever we are implementing method overloading we are going to achieve Static Polymorphism.
[02:19] Here you can see I have given an example.
[02:22] First I'm trying to create the object of this Example class, followed by I'm trying to invoke all these
[02:28] three methods.
[02:29] When I'm trying to invoke these three methods, I'm passing the method input parameter value as per
[02:35] the method definition.
[02:36] If I pass the int value, the very first method is going to be invoked, whereas when I pass the double
[02:42] value, the second method is going to be invoked.
[02:45] And when I pass the String data, the last method is going to be invoked.
[02:49] So the compiler, it is going to take the decision about which method to invoke at the compile time
[02:55] itself.
[02:56] So you can see here the same print() method
[02:58] it is trying to behave differently based upon different input that we are passing at the compile time
[03:05] itself.
[03:06] That's why we can call this kind of Polymorphism as Static Polymorphism.
[03:10] So there won't be any confusion to the compiler to which method it has to call, because all your overloaded
[03:16] methods always they are going to have different method signatures.
[03:20] Now let me show you another example where we have the inheritance implemented.

[03:39] first I have a override method because you will be able to see that I have used the annotation at symbol

[03:46] On top of that, this method signature is exactly same as the method signature that we have inside the

[04:11] we are accepting String and the int as an method input parameters.
[04:16] So the last two methods that we have inside the IronMan, they are overloaded methods because they
[04:22] have different method input parameters compared to the parent method are inherited method inside the
[04:30] IronMan subclass.
[04:31] So whenever you have confusion to understand whether a method is overloaded or not, you can follow
[04:37] a simple rule.
[04:38] First, you can write down the method name followed by a separator like comma or percentage,
[04:44] whatever works for you.
[04:45] After mentioning the method name, you can also mention the data type of your method input parameters.

[04:54] also you can separate them with the help of a separator like comma.

[04:59] this method
