LECTURE: Method overriding vs Method overloading
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Since method overriding and method overloading concepts are very important inside Java, let's try to
[00:06] put more efforts on trying to understand what is the difference between these two concepts.
[00:13] People may get confused very easily at these concepts and inside interviews.
[00:18] Also, the interviewer, he or she can try to confuse you very easily.
[00:22] So to avoid these kind of scenarios, let's try to put some efforts on understanding the differences
[00:29] between method overriding and method overloading.
[00:32] The very first difference is method overriding always happens if a class declares a method that shares
[00:39] the same name, along with the same number of method parameters and same parameter data types in the
[00:46] same order as specified by its superclass, whereas the method overloading is going to happen if multiple
[00:54] methods inside a class have a same name, and all these methods which are sharing the same method name
[01:01] if they have difference in at least one aspect, like it can be a number of method input parameters
[01:08] or their data types are in their order.
[01:11] So in such scenarios the method overloading is going to happen.
[01:15] So these are the definitions of method overriding and a method overloading.
[01:20] Moving on to the second difference.
[01:21] Whenever you want to perform the method overriding, you should always have followed the inheritance.
[01:27] That means you should always have at least two classes,
[01:30] one is superclass and the other one is subclass
[01:34] in order to implement method overriding concept. On the contrast side, you can try to implement method
[01:40] overloading in a single class without worrying about the inheritance.
[01:45] The third difference is the return type of the overridden method must be same as the superclass method,
[01:53] or it should be compatible with the return type of the superclass method.
[01:57] When I say compatible, it should be one of the subtypes of the return type mentioned inside the superclass,
[02:04] whereas inside the method overloading the return type of the method is not going to be considered,
[02:10] and it is not going to influence method overloading concept.
[02:13] On the similar lines, while you are trying to implement method overriding, you are not allowed to
[02:18] include any additional throws class compared to the overriding method.
[02:23] If needed, you can get rid of all the checked exceptions defined inside the superclass method, or
[02:30] you can maintain the same number of checked exceptions or less
[02:33] number of checked exceptions or
[02:35] if needed
[02:36] you can also maintain a different checked exception, but you need to make sure it is one of the subclass
[02:42] of the checked exception, which is defined inside the superclass method on the method overloading
[02:47] side
[02:47] the Throws class is not going to play any role, and it is not going to impact the process of overloading.
[02:54] And the last difference that we have is the method overriding is always applicable for the instance
[03:00] methods or non-static methods, whereas method overloading is applicable for any type of method, whether
[03:08] it is an static method or a non-static method, I can define multiple static methods in a same class
[03:15] with the same name, but with a different method input parameters.
[03:19] So that is perfectly possible with the method overloading.
[03:23] Whereas if you try to overload a static method present inside a superclass in the subclass, then it
[03:30] is not allowed or we cannot call that concept as method overriding.
[03:34] So there is a different concept called method hiding, which you are going to discuss in the coming
[03:39] lectures.
[03:40] And at last I want to highlight you that method overloading is always going to be resolved at compile
[03:46] time based upon the static binding or compile time binding or static polymorphism.
[03:52] And the other side method overriding is always going to be resolved at runtime based upon that dynamic
[03:58] binding or dynamic polymorphism.
[04:00] With this, I'm assuming you are clear about what is method overriding and method overloading.

[00:00] As of now

[00:35] inside Java, we are going to use the this keyword whenever we want to access a member of a current
[00:41] object, whereas super keyword we need to use if we want to access a member of a super class object.
[00:48] For example
[00:49] here you can see I have given two different examples.

[01:17] that I have created at the top of the class, whereas with the other name variable, we are trying to
[01:23] refer to the parameter that we have received as an input to this constructor.
[01:27] So with this, it should be clear for you.
[01:29] Whenever we want to access a member of a current object, we should be using the this keyword.
[01:35] Whereas super keyword will always come into picture in the scenarios of inheritance.

[02:15] the superclass.

[03:02] subclass constructor.
[03:03] At last, I want to highlight you that both these this and super keywords.

[03:10] We can't use them as an variable identifiers or method name identifiers.

[01:39] classes.

[02:58] inside the Java library before Java 8, there are thousands of interfaces inside the Java library.
[03:03] Java team
[03:04] when they decided to introduce new features into these interfaces, they immediately faced the problem
[03:11] in all the subclasses with the compilation error.
[03:14] And all these Java interfaces might be being used by many of the organizations in their own business
[03:21] logic.

LECTURE: Jagged Arrays
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside this lecture, let's try to understand about a flavor of two dimensional array which is jagged
[00:07] arrays.
[00:07] So what are jagged arrays?
[00:09] As of now we are trying to create two dimensional array where each row, they are going to have a fixed
[00:16] number of columns.
[00:17] That means we are maintaining uniformity across sub arrays or across nested arrays.
[00:24] However, Java also provides a concept of jagged arrays, and whenever you are building a two dimensional
[00:32] array which is going to contain sub arrays with varying sizes, such kind of two dimensional arrays,
[00:39] we are going to call them as jagged arrays.
[00:42] For example, you can see I'm trying to create a jagged array, and this jagged array is a two dimensional
[00:48] array.

[01:22] lecture is, this approach is capable of reading a single character, a word, a sentence, a file,

[01:53] class.

[03:05] you can see by default, whenever we are trying to create this BufferReader object, it is going to
[03:10] have a buffer size of eight kilobytes or 800192 bytes capacity.
[03:16] So the purpose of this buffer size is think like you're trying to provide a file to this BufferReader
[03:22] object to read the data.
[03:24] So inside your file you may have hundreds or thousands of lines.
[03:28] If you don't have this buffer size concept, this BufferReader object, it is going to end up reading
[03:35] character by character from your file.
[03:37] So every time you want to read a character, it will go to your file.
[03:41] It will read the character and it will load into the memory.

[03:50] So to overcome these challenges, Java team decided to provide some buffer capacity to the BufferReader
[03:57] object.
[03:57] So with this capacity what is going to happen is your BufferReader object

[04:04] So whenever it is trying to go and read the content inside a file, it is going to load 8kb of
[04:11] data at once into the memory location and post that it is going to process character by character from
[04:19] the memory itself.
[04:20] So processing of the data from the memory is more faster compared to the reading of the data from the
[04:26] file which is present inside the disk.
[04:28] If needed
[04:29] we can also change these buffer size.
[04:31] Maybe if you are trying to read a very big file, you can try to improve these buffer size with the
[04:37] help of the second constructor.
[04:39] So whenever you are trying to create the object of BufferReader, you can try to provide the object
[04:44] of Reader.
[04:45] And the second parameter is size
[04:47] but for the most of the scenarios, this default size should be good enough, like 8192.
[04:53] If needed, you can increase based upon your business requirements in real projects.
[04:58] So now I'm assuming
[04:59] you are clear why these processes are efficient, especially while reading the data from the file.
[05:05] Maybe when you are trying to access the data from an end user.
[05:09] Maybe in those scenarios, these buffer size may not be super helpful because the end user at max he
[05:14] may enter a value, a character, or a word or a sentence.

LECTURE: Comparison of BufferedReader and Scanner
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Let's try to understand the differences between BufferReader and Scanner approaches.
[00:05] Most of these differences we already discussed in the previous lectures, but there is no harm in revising
[00:11] one more time.
[00:12] The very first difference is whenever you are trying to use a BufferReader, it is only capable of
[00:17] reading the sequence of characters in a String format.
[00:20] Once the reading operation is completed, it is going to be the responsibility of the developer to convert
[00:26] that String object data into an corresponding output format like int, double, float based upon the business
[00:34] requirements of the developer.
[00:35] Whereas with the scanner we have various methods which are going to start with a prefix and next.
[00:42] So based upon the type of input data that we are trying to accept, we can invoke these next methods
[00:48] to get the output in various formats like int, short, byte, float, long, double, String, boolean.
[00:55] So please use them based upon your business requirements.
[00:58] The second difference, like you know, BufferReader is present inside the Java right from day one,
[01:05] whereas Scanner is introduced only from the JDK 1.5 release.
[01:11] So why Java team release Scanner?
[01:13] Since there are some drawbacks, and since there is some complexity in using BufferReader, they want
[01:19] to make the life of developers easy.
[01:21] That's why they have introduced Scanner under the java.util package as part of the 1.5 version.
[01:28] The next major difference that we have is BufferReader
[01:31] has a capability to hold the large buffer size, which is by default eight kilobytes, whereas
[01:38] with the Scanner the buffer size is going to be only 1kb.
[01:43] Apart from these buffer size differences, BufferReader allows you to customize this buffer size based
[01:49] upon your business requirements.
[01:51] If these 8kb is not sufficient, you can try to create the object of BufferReader with a buffer
[01:57] size of 16 kb or any amount of large buffer size, and the other side the Scanner.
[02:03] It is not going to provide you that flexibility.
[02:06] It is always going to allow you to create an object of Scanner with the default buffer size, which
[02:12] is 1kb.
[02:13] With these differences, it should be pretty clear for you when you are dealing with the large amount
[02:18] of data, like you're trying to read the data from a huge file.
[02:22] In such scenarios, the BufferReader is the most suitable one compared to the Scanner, because BufferReader
[02:28] at a time, it can load the data of around 8kb, whereas Scanner is only capable of
[02:36] 1kb.
[02:36] So due to these size differences, Scanner always has a disadvantage whenever you are trying to deal
[02:42] with the large files or large input data, whereas for a short input data or a small input files, you
[02:50] can happily use Scanner and there won't be any performance issue.
[02:54] The next difference is around the synchronization.
[02:57] Inside Java, there is a concept of multithreading.
[03:00] We are going to discuss in the coming sections.
[03:03] What is multithreading?
[03:04] Multithreading is a concept where your program is going to be executed at a single time by multiple
[03:10] threads, or by multiple requests, which are invoked by multiple end users.
[03:15] In such scenarios, it is always safe to use BufferReader because it is a synchronized class, which
[03:22] means you can share the same BufferReader object across multiple threads.
[03:27] Whereas Scanner is not a synchronized class, you cannot share this Scanner object across multiple threads.
[03:34] So if you are developing a business logic for a multithreading environment, always consider
[03:41] BufferReader.
[03:41] The next difference we have is around the exception handling.
[03:44] BufferReader always force you to handle the IOException, either by mentioning the throws statement
[03:51] inside the method signature, or with the help of exception handling techniques, which you are going
[03:56] to discuss in the coming sections.
[03:57] Whereas scanner does not force the developer to handle the IOException, it is going to hide it and
[04:03] behind the scenes it is going to handle this exception.
[04:07] And at last we can say BufferReader is faster and efficient because it supports larger buffer size
[04:14] of 8KB and if needed we can further increase it, whereas Scanner is slower and less efficient.
[04:20] That's why always please note that if you are dealing with a small input data, you can happily use
[04:26] the Scanner.
[04:27] Whereas if you are trying to deal with the large input data like large files, like 1MB, 2MB
[04:34] files, then in such scenarios always go with the BufferReader.
[04:38] I hope you are clear with these differences.
[04:40] These differences are very important from interview perspective.
[04:44] So people can always ask you what are the differences between them and under which scenarios.
[04:49] We should use BufferReader and Scanner.
[04:51] So these kind of questions you should be able to easily answer with the discussion that we had throughout
[04:57] this lecture.
[04:58] Thank you and I'll catch you in the
[04:59] next lecture bye.

LECTURE: Don’t use System.out.println in Production code
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, we discussed a lot of concepts and topics inside Java.
[00:05] With all the knowledge that we have gained so far by this time, you might have became a fan to the
[00:10] System.out.println(), and you may have intentions to use this a lot inside your real projects as well.
[00:18] But I want you to stop there and I want to give you a cautious note here, which is it is not recommended
[00:24] to use the System.out.println() or any other print methods inside production code.
[00:31] What is the meaning of production code?
[00:33] Whenever you are building the Java logic or any code for a real application which will be deployed eventually
[00:40] into your production environment in the form of website or in the form of mobile application, or in
[00:45] the form of a API service.
[00:47] Regardless of how your code is deployed, it is always considered as a production code because your
[00:54] code is going to be served to the actual end users.
[00:58] So in all these kind of production related scenarios, we are not allowed to use a System.out,.println().
[01:05] We should only use this during learning Java, or whenever you are trying to debug your code, or whenever
[01:11] you are trying to test your code.
[01:13] In those scenarios only we are supposed to use this, but not in the production code.
[01:17] With that definitely you might have surprised and you may have questions.
[01:23] Why should I not use a System.out.println() ?
[01:26] Let me try to explain what are the drawbacks that we have.
[01:29] If we use the System.out dot.println(), your compiler is not going to stop you.
[01:34] You can always mention System.out.println().
[01:37] In fact, even today there are many developers who use these System.out.println() unknowingly inside their
[01:44] production code.
[01:45] But inside the projects where a strong review process is established.
[01:50] In this kind of projects, the lead or the senior developer who is trying to perform a code review of
[01:56] a junior developer if he sees this System.out.println().
[01:59] Which is trying to get pushed into the production code in such scenarios, they will definitely blame
[02:04] you and they will give a code review comment saying that remove these System.out.println().
[02:10] So I don't want you to be into that embarrassing situations.
[02:14] That's why let's try to understand why we should not use them and what are the alternatives that we
[02:19] have.
[02:19] The very first drawback using System.out.println() is, performance degradation.
[02:25] If you write a small program with the System.out.println() are two different places, nothing is going
[02:31] to happen.
[02:32] It is not going to impact your application in any way, but in real projects there will be thousands
[02:38] of classes and inside these thousands of classes, there will be millions of lines of code in all these
[02:44] millions of lines of code.
[02:45] If each developer end up using System.out.println(), wherever he wants will be, end up having thousands
[02:52] of System.out.println() statements.
[02:54] And with that, it is going to have a performance degradation problem inside your application, especially
[03:00] while we are trying to print the a large message.
[03:04] Why there will be a performance degradation.
[03:06] Because whenever you want to print a big message onto your console like we discussed previously, first
[03:12] it has to get an object of PrintStream.
[03:16] So when this object of PrintStream is getting created, a connection to your console will be opened
[03:22] behind the scenes.
[03:22] And with that connection, only the message will be printed onto the console.
[03:26] And at last, the connection with the console, which is established by the PrintStream object, has
[03:31] to be closed behind the scenes, since these kind of operations are happening behind the scenes, so
[03:37] there is a good chance that a performance degradation can happen.
[03:41] The second disadvantage is lack of flexibility.
[03:44] Whenever you are trying to print a message to the console, you will have very limited control on how
[03:50] you can format your message.
[03:53] Especially you can't add the details like under which method, under which class the printing of the
[03:58] statement happened, at which point of time, and using which thread.
[04:02] So all these kind of information you will not be able to print with the help of System.out.println()
[04:09] statements.
[04:10] Believe me, in real projects the logging requirements are even more complex.
[04:15] When I say logging.
[04:16] What is the meaning of logging?
[04:18] Logging is the process of printing a value onto the console or onto a file, which we can use at later
[04:26] point of time to debug what happened inside our program.
[04:30] So in real projects, the logging requirements are going to be super complex.
[04:34] All such complex requirements can't be achieved with the help of System.out.println().
[04:40] And the third disadvantage is inability to disable logging.
[04:44] When I try to print a message with the help of System.out.println(), there is no way for me to disable
[04:51] that printing other than deleting the entire line of System.out.println().
[04:57] Whereas with the alternatives that we are going.
[05:00] To discuss in the coming lectures.
[05:02] They're going to provide you an ability to disable your logging if it is on.
[05:07] The logging is going to happen if it is off.
[05:10] In such scenarios, the logging is not going to happen.
[05:13] So it is a kind of having a control to disable the logging whenever you want.
[05:18] Whereas with System.out.println() we will not have any such control
[05:22] always
[05:22] the only option to disable the logging with the help of System.out.println() is to delete the code itself
[05:29] and at last using the System.out.println() will have some security risks, especially if you try
[05:35] to log the sensitive information such as passwords, personal data, health data.
[05:41] So all these details
[05:42] if you try to print into the console, it can pose a security risk as anyone who has access to your
[05:49] console can see the information.
[05:51] So using System.out.println(), we can only log the output into the console.
[05:57] So anyone who has access to the server where it is deployed, they will be able to easily see the sensitive
[06:03] information that is logged.
[06:04] So with all these we should always not use the System.out.println() inside production code.
[06:11] Instead we should look for the advanced options.
[06:14] So what are these advanced options?
[06:16] We should use the logging frameworks.
[06:19] So what is a framework?
[06:20] A framework is a project or a library which is focused to solve a given problem with less effort.
[06:28] So to overcome all the drawbacks of System.out.println(), there are good amount of logging frameworks
[06:33] available inside the Java ecosystem.
[06:35] The Java library itself.
[06:37] It has a package with the name java.util.logging.
[06:41] Inside this package we have logging related classes which we can use to perform the logging, and apart
[06:47] from these basic support of logging from the Java, we also have dedicated logging frameworks like
[06:54] Log4j, SLF4J.
[06:56] So these are the most advanced logging frameworks.
[06:59] And they allow you to configure logging levels, log rotation, log aggregation and more.
[07:06] So what is logging levels?
[07:07] I'm going to discuss about logging levels in the coming lectures.
[07:11] Log rotation and log aggregation is a process where these frameworks, they will allow you to log your
[07:17] output data into a log file.
[07:20] So if you keep appending the log data to a single log file at some point of time, it can become
[07:26] 2GB, 5GB or 1TB text file and you will not be able to open such files.
[07:31] So that's why these frameworks to avoid these kind of challenges, they provide you log rotation and
[07:38] log aggregation.
[07:40] So whenever we are using these logging frameworks we can configure these frameworks such a way that
[07:45] every one hour or every five minutes you can create a new file.
[07:49] And the logging is going to happen in the new log file that got created.
[07:53] I'm not going to focus a lot about the logging frameworks inside this course, because these are super
[07:59] advanced topics
[08:00] and since right now we are focusing on the Java programming language, I'm just giving some hints around
[08:06] what are the best practices that you need to follow so that you can become a good developer inside your
[08:12] projects.
[08:13] Once you master Java, obviously, as a next step, you're going to learn frameworks like spring spring
[08:18] boot microservices.
[08:20] During your advanced journey inside the spring ecosystem, you should also learn one of the logging
[08:27] framework.
[08:27] For example, inside my Spring Spring Boot related course, I have discussed in detail about the logging

[08:54] is possible, we can use the logging.

LECTURE: Logging in Java - Part 1
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside this lecture, I'm going to show you a demo of logging for the same
[00:04] first I'm going to create a new package and the package name is going to be com.eazybytes.log

[00:15] first I'm going to create a new Java class.

[00:22] first I'm going to create a main() method.

[00:30] we need to make sure we are creating the object of Logger by using the classes available inside that
[00:37] Java library to create the object of Logger, we're not going to use a new operator or the constructor
[00:43] of the Logger class.
[00:44] Instead, we need to create the Logger object as an static variable.

[00:00] It might be a super surprising fact for you that our programs are throwing runtime exceptions, but

[00:12] Java.
[00:13] To handle the exceptions, we need to build the try and catch block inside our Java code.
[00:19] We know that an exception is an event that can occurs during the execution of a program that is going
[00:26] to disrupt the normal flow of the program
[00:29] instructions.
[00:30] Let's see how to handle a runtime exception.
[00:33] Whenever you are trying to write a piece of logic inside a Java method, which may potentially throw
[00:39] an exception at runtime, all such code, you need to define them inside that try block.
[00:45] So how to define a try block?
[00:47] First you need to mention the try keyword, followed by the opening and closing curly braces.
[00:52] Inside this try block, you can write all your Java code which you feel it is a risky code, even if
[00:59] you have 1% of doubt on your code that it may throw an exception, then it is always advisable to keep
[01:06] all such code inside the try block immediately after the try block, you should also write the catch
[01:12] block.
[01:12] So what is the purpose of catch block?
[01:14] Inside the catch block, we are going to write the logic that needs to be executed in case of a runtime
[01:21] exception happens.
[01:22] So if you closely look at the screenshot that I have provided in the slide, the format that you need
[01:27] to follow to define a catch block is, first you need to mention the catch keyword, followed by inside
[01:33] the parentheses you need to mention what is the exception type.
[01:38] Are you talking about an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or are you talking about
[01:44] InputMismatchDataException.
[01:45] Are you talking about a NullPointerException.
[01:47] So you need to define your exception type along with a object reference of it.
[01:52] Post that inside the curly braces of your catch block
[01:55] you can write all the code that needs to be executed in case of a runtime exception happens based upon
[02:03] the code that is being executed inside the try block.

LECTURE: [JAVA 7] multiple catch blocks - Part 2
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Sometimes, while we are trying to define multiple catch blocks to handle different kinds of exceptions
[00:07] with a different exception handling logic, you may have a requirement which is to have a same exception
[00:14] handling for few set off exceptions.
[00:17] For example, as of now you can see we have a catch block to catch an exception of StringIndexOut
[00:22] StringIndexOutofBoundsException.
[00:23] Very similarly, I may want to add one more catch block to handle the exception, which is array index
[00:31] ArrayIndexOutofBoundsException.
[00:32] Think like for a second that we want to have a same business logic are same exception handling logic
[00:39] to be executed for these two exceptions because they both extend the same class like index out of bound
[00:47] IndexOutofBoundException.
[00:47] So these kind of exception happens whenever you are trying to access an index which is not available.
[00:54] It can be inside an Array or it can be inside String object.
[00:57] That's why having a same business logic or same exception handling logic for these kind of exceptions
[01:03] makes sense.
[01:04] So in these kind of scenarios, instead of repeating that two catch blocks multiple times, we can have
[01:11] a single catch block which is capable of handling multiple exceptions.
[01:15] Let me show you how to achieve the same.
[01:17] So to handle multiple exceptions with a single catch block, you need to use the pipe symbol after an
[01:25] exception data type.
[01:26] As of now you can see I have the first exception data type as StringIndexOutofBoundsException.
[01:31] After mentioning the space pipe symbol, I need to mention one more space and post that I can mention.
[01:37] What is a second exception.
[01:39] So with this
[01:40] single catch block is capable of handling both these exceptions that we have configured here.
[01:46] We are getting a compilation error here because we already handled these exception in the second catch
[01:52] block.
[01:52] That's why let me remove this and post that
[01:55] I'm going to update the statement as IndexOutofBoundsException occurred.
[02:01] Please check your input data so the data can be it can be a string data or it can be an array data.
[02:07] That's why I'm trying to have a generic statement here for these two kinds of exception.
[02:12] So the syntax that we are discussing right now, which we can mention multiple exceptions in a catch
[02:17] block with the help of a pipe symbol, is introduced as part of the java7.
[02:23] Before Java seven, developers are forced to define multiple catch blocks, even though the business
[02:29] logic or the exception handling logic is same for different exceptions.
[02:33] But from java7, we can happily use this syntax that right now we are discussing.
[02:38] And here you should not be under the assumption that we can only handle two exceptions.
[02:42] With this kind of syntax, we can handle any kind of exceptions with this pipe symbol.
[02:48] For example, after the ArrayIndexOutofBoundsException, I can mention the space pipe symbol space,
[02:55] and I can mention some other exception.
[02:57] Like I can try to mention some other exception which is InputMismatchException.
[03:02] This way we can add any number of exceptions to the same catch block.
[03:08] By using these pipe symbol and all these exceptions, they are going to have a single object reference
[03:14] variable name which is ex, because at any time your code is going to throw only one type of exception,
[03:22] but not all three types of exception.
[03:24] In the scenario where your code is going to throw InputMismatchException, then this ex object reference
[03:30] it is going to hold the object of InputMismatchException class.
[03:35] There is a guideline or a restriction that you need to be aware whenever you are using this syntax.
[03:40] The restriction is whatever object reference that you are trying to assign to these multiple exceptions.
[03:47] Inside your catch block, this is going to be final.
[03:50] You will not be able to assign a new value to these ex object inside the catch block body.
[03:57] For example, I can show you a demo.
[03:58] Before that, let me remove this unnecessary exception that we have here.
[04:03] Post that inside the catch block body, I'm going to assign a new object of some exception like
[04:10] ArrayIndexOutofBoundException.
[04:12] With that, you can see we are getting a compilation error saying that cannot assign a value to the
[04:17] final variable ex.
[04:18] We didn't mention final before this ex, but behind the scenes, whenever you are going to use this syntax,
[04:25] the object reference, it is going to be implicitly final.
[04:29] That's why we are seeing a restriction here, which is we are not able to assign a new value to the
[04:35] object reference that we have defined inside this catch block.

LECTURE: Differences between throw and throws keyword

[00:00] There are a good amount of differences between throw and throws

[00:10] we can manually throw an exception when an error or unexpected situation arises, and we can use this
[00:18] throw keyword only inside a method body.
[00:21] Whereas coming to the throws keyword, throws keyword is used in the method signature to indicate that
[00:28] a given method may throw list of exceptions due to certain statements or actions within its body.
[00:35] So please be very clear about the placements.
[00:38] Throw can always be used inside the method body, whereas throws can be used only in the method signature.
[00:44] Now coming to the syntax on how to use these keywords whenever we are using the throw keyword, after
[00:51] mentioning the throw keyword, we need to provide an object or an instance of an Exception class.

[01:04] object.

[01:32] a subclass of Throwable class, which is a superclass for all the exceptions and errors inside the Java
[01:39] library.

LECTURE: Exception Propagation
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Let me explain about what is an Exception Propagation
[00:04] Inside this lecture. We know whenever an exception is being thrown from a method, and if the same
[00:10] is not being catched or caught within that method, then the exception will try to propagate to the
[00:16] calling method.
[00:17] So this process continues until the exception is properly handled with the help of a catch block or
[00:25] it reaches the top level method.
[00:28] So what will be the top level method inside our Java programs?
[00:31] It is main() method in the case of an unchecked exception, being trying to propagate to the caller methods
[00:39] or the parent methods, then in such scenarios, there is no mandatory to have a throws statement or
[00:45] to have a catch block, so the unchecked exception eventually it will propagate to the top level method
[00:51] or a main() method.
[00:52] Whereas in the scenario of checked exceptions, since the compiler is going to force the programmers
[00:58] to handle the checked exceptions either with the help of throws or with the help of catch block.
[01:03] In the case of checked exceptions, the exception will try to propagate to the nearest catch block,
[01:09] or it will keep propagating to the main() method or the top level method.

LECTURE: Nested try block
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Just like how we can write a nested if block nested for loop nested while loops.
[00:06] Very similarly, inside Java we can define nested try blocks as well.
[00:11] For example, here you can see a sample code that I have written.
[00:15] So there is a main try block which is trying to execute a piece of code.
[00:20] And to this main try block we have a catch block which is handling the exception with the object reference
[00:27] name as Ee3.
[00:28] Inside this main try block we have statement one and statement two.
[00:32] But when we are trying to execute this statement three and statement four, we have another nested try
[00:39] block.
[00:39] The reason why we will develop these kind of nested try blocks is,
[00:43] imagine if there is an exception happens inside this statement three or statement 4.
[00:48] In such scenarios, we don't want to affect the execution of our try block.
[00:53] Maybe after these second try block at the end, I may have other statements like statement 7, statement 8.
[01:00] .
[01:01] So if I want to make sure that the statements that I'm trying to execute as part of this second try
[01:07] block should not affect the execution of the statements that I have inside the outer try block.
[01:11] In such scenarios, we can use this nested try block concept.
[01:16] So inside the second try block I'm trying to execute statement 3 and statement 4.
[01:20] If there is an exception happen at this point of time, the catch block with the object reference e1
[01:27] is going to handle the same.
[01:28] And inside the second try block I have another nested third try block.
[01:33] So it is going to execute the statements with the number statement 5 and statement 6.
[01:38] If there is some issue happen at this point of time, the innermost catch block with the object reference
[01:45] e2, it is going to handle the exception.
[01:47] So this way we can always write any levels of nested try blocks.
[01:53] The purpose of nested try block is we don't want to propagate the exception to the outer try block,
[01:59] or to the method.

LECTURE: final, finally and finalize
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside Java, there are three different similar jargons that you may hear a lot
[00:05] many times these are final,
[00:08] finally, finalize.
[00:09] Though they are looking very similar, but there is a lot of difference between them and the scenarios where
[00:15] we are going to use them also vary a lot.
[00:18] Since this is a topic where students can easily get confused, I want to spend a few minutes explaining
[00:24] you about the differences between final, finally and finalize, and this is also a favorite question
[00:31] for the most of the interviewers.
[00:33] That's why
[00:34] please be attentive to this lecture, and with that, any confusions that you may have around these
[00:39] jargons will get cleared.
[00:41] The very first jargon or
[00:43] the keyword that you can see here is final.
[00:45] So what is the purpose of final inside Java?
[00:47] Using final we can declare final constant values or final methods under final Java class.
[00:56] Whenever we are using this final keyword to declare a variable or to declare a constant value, such
[01:03] variables are such constants
[01:05] we can't update them, or we can't reinitialize them with a different value at later point of time
[01:11] inside the program. Whatever you are going to provide during the initialization, the same value is
[01:18] going to be final.
[01:19] For example, inside this program you can see I'm trying to declare a variable x along with the final
[01:25] keyword, and inside this x I have stored the value five.
[01:28] With that, I will not be able to update these x variable with some other value inside the program at
[01:34] later point of time.
[01:35] The compiler is not going to allow this.
[01:38] Similarly, whenever we are defining the final keyword as part of the method signature, then such methods
[01:44] behavior or the logic cannot be overrided by the subclasses.
[01:49] All the subclasses
[01:50] they have to simply accept whatever business logic defined inside the final method of a superclass.
[01:56] And at last we can also mention this final keyword as part of the class definition.
[02:01] Whenever we are mentioning the final keyword as part of the class definition, then in such scenarios,
[02:06] your class is not going to support any inheritance, no other subclass.
[02:11] they can extend your class as a superclass.
[02:14] So we are trying to completely disable the inheritance behavior with the help of final keyword inside
[02:21] the class definition.
[02:22] Now moving on to the next jargon, which is finally.
[02:25] We just now discussed inside this section where we talked about how to perform the exception handling.
[02:32] Whenever you are trying to define, try and catch blocks in such scenarios, we can define the finally
[02:38] blocks using finally keyword
[02:40] we can build the finally blocks we already discussed
[02:43] what is the purpose of finally block?
[02:45] With the help of finally block, we can specify a block of code that is going to be executed regardless
[02:51] of whether an exception is thrown or caught in the try or catch blocks.
[02:56] This finally block ensures that the code that you have written inside them, such as closing a database
[03:02] connection or releasing a lock.
[03:04] So all these kind of code, it is always going to be executed in both kind of scenarios like happy scenario
[03:11] and exception scenario.
[03:12] Now moving on to the last jargon which is finalize.
[03:16] Finalize is a method available inside the object superclass.
[03:21] We know inside Java there is a garbage collector which is responsible to clean up the object that are
[03:28] no longer being used.
[03:29] So with the help of garbage collection, the memory occupied by the unused objects inside the heap memory
[03:36] is going to be cleaned or retained regularly.
[03:39] So whenever a garbage collector is trying to remove an unused object from an heap memory.
[03:44] In such scenarios, if you want to perform any cleanup operations, or if you want to release any resources
[03:51] before the object is destroyed in such scenarios inside your class, you can override the method finalize()
[03:58] that is provided by the object superclass.
[04:02] So whatever logic that you are going to write inside this Overrided finalize() method, the same is going
[04:07] to be executed whenever the garbage collection is happening.
[04:11] But please note that JVM is not always going to invoke your finalize() method.
[04:16] It is not going to guarantee that it is always going to invoke the finalize() method that you have defined
[04:23] whenever a class object is being destroyed.
[04:25] In fact, this finalize() method is deprecated.
[04:29] Let me show you that very quickly.
[04:31] First, let me open the Object superclass.
[04:34] So this is the superclass for all the classes inside Java.
[04:38] So if you see there is a method called finalize().
[04:40] As of now it is empty.
[04:42] If needed we can override these method inside our respective Java classes.
[04:48] But these methods you can see it is deprecated from Java 9.
[04:51] And this is going to be removed in the near future permanently from the Java library.
[04:57] We can also see some documentation
[04:59] around this.
[05:00] After this deprecated you will be able to read this information.
[05:03] Finalization is deprecated and subject to removal in a future release.
[05:08] The use of finalization can lead to problems with the security, performance and reliability.
[05:13] That's why they are trying to remove these.
[05:16] For now
[05:16] they mark this method as deprecated.
[05:18] With that you may have a question.
[05:20] Then what is the alternative for these finalize() method?
[05:23] The alternative options are also highlighted here.
[05:25] Inside the documentation they clearly highlighted use java.lang.ref.Cleaner() and
[05:32] java.lang.ref.Phantom() reference as a safer ways to release resources whenever an object becomes unreachable.
[05:40] So these are the alternatives.
[05:41] But for now, let's not worry about these advanced topics or the alternative options we are right now

[03:30] That means if you are trying to invoke the equals() method with the help of object A, by passing the
[03:37] object to be as an input.

[04:01] input.

[04:19] That means if a.equals(b) is true and b.equals(c) is true, then a.equals(c) should also be
[04:29] true.
[04:29] If there are three different objects with the name a, b, c are involved.
[04:34] If a.equals(b) is resulting into true and b.equals(c) is also resulting in true, then obviously
[04:42] you should also get the a.equals(c) also as true.
[04:46] And the fourth rule says consistency.
[04:48] That means the equals() method should always give the consistent results, even if you try to invoke it
[04:55] multiple times as long as the objects are not
[04:59] modified.
[05:00] And the fifth rule is we should make sure we are handling the null.
[05:03] It's common to check for null to avoid NullPointerException in the equals() method.
[05:08] So we have handled the null check as part of the second if condition, like you can see here this second
[05:15] if condition it has one of the check where it is going to check the null check.
[05:20] And the second object that we have received the same is being conveyed with these rule number five.
[05:26] And the rule number six is the equals() method has a strong relationship or tight coupling with the hashCode()
[05:32] method.
[05:32] So that's why whenever you are trying to override the equals() method, you should also make sure you
[05:38] are overriding the hashCode() method with the same object instance variables or the object parameters.
[05:44] And like we discussed in the previous lectures, whenever the a.equals(b) evaluates to true, then
[05:51] the hashCode() calculation of the a object and the b object should be same, but the reverse of it does
[05:57] not always result into true.

LECTURE: Deep dive on finalize() in Object class
----------------------------------------

[00:00] We talked briefly about the finalized() method in the previous section when we were trying to compare
[00:05] with the final keyword and the finally block.
[00:08] But now let's try to discuss in detail about the purpose of this finalized() method.
[00:14] In Java, it is very normal that an Java object.
[00:17] Sometimes it may consume some resources, or it may open some connection with resources like files or
[00:24] a database.
[00:24] So in all these kind of scenarios, whenever an object is trying to consume a resource, it is always
[00:30] a good practice to release these resources whenever it is no longer needed by your object to achieve
[00:36] the same.
[00:37] The Java language offers a mechanism to perform the cleanup or resource releasing just before the object
[00:44] is destroyed or discarded by the garbage collector.
[00:48] We know inside Java, we as a Java developers, we are only allowed to create the objects and there
[00:54] is no need of manually destroying the objects or destructing the objects inside the heap
[00:59] memory.
[00:59] We are not allowed to do that because behind the scenes, the Java virtual machine, it is going to

[01:12] are no longer needed.

LECTURE: Details about Shallow cloning & Deep cloning - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] In Java
[00:01] there are two types of cloning that we can perform.
[00:03] The very first one is Shallow cloning and the second one is Deep cloning.
[00:08] Let's try to understand what are these cloning and how they work.
[00:12] These are the very important topics.
[00:14] If you go to any Java related interviews, anyone can answer questions around the clone() method.
[00:20] But if someone wants to test your deep knowledge inside Java, they can ask some difficult questions
[00:26] around shallow cloning and deep cloning.
[00:28] That's why, my friend, my request is please pay attention and try to understand what is this
[00:34] Shallow cloning and Deep cloning.
[00:35] This shallow cloning and deep cloning only come into picture if a given object has some other embedded
[00:42] objects.
[00:43] In the previous lecture, we have a Person class, and inside this Person class we only have primitive
[00:49] data type instance fields along with that String object.
[00:52] Other than that, we don't have any other complex objects, but in real projects we always have embedded
[00:59] objects as an instance.
[01:01] Variables inside your own class, I'm going to show you what do I mean by embedded objects in few seconds.
[01:07] But before that, let's try to understand what is a shallow cloning.
[01:10] Whenever you're trying to perform cloning with the help of shallow cloning, it is going to create the
[01:15] new copy of your outer object only, but it is not going to create the copies of the embedded objects
[01:22] referenced by the original object.
[01:24] Instead, it is going to simply copy the reference of the embedded objects.
[01:29] For example, like you can see here, I have a Student class, and inside this Student class I have
[01:35] instance variables name and course.
[01:38] So this course is a instance variable which belongs to other class with the name course.
[01:44] So inside this course class I have another instance variable which is courseName.
[01:49] So with this code my Student class object it is going to have an embedded object of Course class.
[01:56] If you try to override the clone() method inside the Student class like you can see here, we simply override
[02:04] the clone() method and we are trying to invoke the clone() method with the help of super.clone().
[02:08] So this is a classical example of shallow cloning.
[02:12] So with this shallow cloning, what is going to happen behind the scenes inside the heap memory is you're
[02:17] going to have an original student.
[02:19] And if you try to clone this original student object, you're going to get another cloned student physical
[02:25] object.
[02:26] They both are stored in two different memory locations, but coming to the embedded objects, like course,
[02:32] both these original student object and the cloned student object, they are going to point to the same
[02:38] course object, because shallow cloning is not capable of copying the embedded objects.
[02:45] Instead, it simply copy the reference of the embedded objects into the objects of original student
[02:52] and the cloned student.
[02:53] This is because we are trying to go with the simple invocation of super.clone().
[02:58] With this, it should be pretty clear for you whenever your class has instance variables, which belongs
[03:03] to other class.
[03:04] In such scenarios, if you are going with the default logic of cloning, you are always going to end
[03:10] up with the shallow cloning.
[03:11] I can also show you an example of shallow cloning based upon these two classes,
[03:16] Student and Course.
[03:17] You can see here inside the main() method.
[03:19] First, I'm trying to create a Course with the variable name as math.
[03:23] Inside this math course, I'm trying to store the course name as math and post that I have created an
[03:29] original student by passing the student name and the course object later on
[03:34] if I try to perform the cloning with the help of original Student object, I'm going to get another
[03:40] object with the name cloned student.
[03:42] So both these original student and the cloned student, they represent two different physical objects.
[03:49] That's why if I try to compare the memory locations of these two objects with the help of these double
[03:54] equal to operator, I'm going to get the output as false because they point to the two different memory
[04:00] locations.
[04:00] Whereas if you try to check the memory location of the Course object which is present inside the original
[04:06] student and the cloned student, you're going to get the output as true, because the same course object
[04:12] is being maintained in both the original student and the cloned student object.
[04:18] I hope you are clear about the shallow cloning.
[04:20] Now let's try to understand what is deep cloning, which means whenever you want to copy the even the
[04:26] embedded objects, then in such scenarios, you need to override the clone() method with a different logic
[04:32] like you can see here
[04:33] first, I'm trying to invoke the super.clone() method, which is going to give me the cloned student
[04:39] object later on
[04:41] I should also perform the cloning of the Course object, which is available inside the same object.
[04:46] So that's why I'm trying to invoke the course.clone(), and the same I'm trying to assign to the
[04:52] clonedStudent.course().
[04:53] And with that, we will end up performing the deep cloning.
[04:57] And this is how it is going to look like inside the
[05:00] heap memory both the original student and the cloned student.
[05:03] They will point to the two different course objects.
[05:07] But before you try to perform this deep cloning, please make sure you also implement Clonable interface
[05:14] inside your Course class.
[05:16] On top of that, you should also overwrite the clone() method with the help of super.clone().
[05:21] Otherwise, when you invoke these clone() method with the help of Course object, you are going to get
[05:26] the CloneNotSupportedException.
[05:28] Let's try to understand the example of deep cloning like you can see here.
[05:32] When we try to perform the cloning of the original student, the student details along with the embedded
[05:38] course details, both of them, they are going to be copied into separate physical memories.
[05:44] That's why for these two statements, we are going to get the output as false because they are pointing
[05:49] to the two different memory locations.
[05:52] I hope you are clear about these theory discussion around the shallow cloning and deep cloning.
[05:57] In the next lecture, let's see the demo of these shallow cloning and deep cloning.

LECTURE: Mutable and Immutable objects - Theory

[00:00] Since we are discussing everything about the objects inside Java inside this section, I think it would
[00:06] be a wise decision to discuss about one more important concept around objects, which is creating mutable
[00:14] and immutable objects in Java.
[00:16] So what are mutable and immutable objects ?
[00:20] In java mutable and immutable terms refer to describe the ability of an object to be modified after it has been
[00:29] created.
[00:30] Immutable objects are the objects whose state or whose data cannot be changed once they are created.
[00:37] If you need to modify an immutable object, it is not going to be possible.
[00:41] The only option is you must create a new object with the required modified state or with the required
[00:50] new data. Whereas on the other hand, we have mutable objects whose state or
[00:55] data can be changed once they are created. With mutable objects
[00:59] we should be able to add new data, modify the existing data, delete the existing data inside the objects
[01:06] without worrying about creating a new instance.
[01:09] So these are basic definition about mutable and immutable objects.

[01:44] use the getter and setter methods.

[06:15] That's a great question.
[06:17] There can be some scenarios where you don't want your object to be modified at later point of program.
[06:23] Maybe think like you have created an object inside method1(), and you are trying to send the object
[06:30] as an input for the other methods like method2(), method3(), method4().
[06:34] So regardless of how many methods your object is going to be passed, you don't want the other methods

[06:43] In such scenarios, we can go with the immutable objects and apart from this, we also have another
[06:49] great reason on building the immutable objects.
[06:53] The reason is due to security reasons.
[06:55] Think like inside your Java application, you are dealing with some sensitive logic or sensitive information.
[07:01] You don't want any other method or any other API inside your project to be able to modify a given object
[07:08] once that is created. If the object can be modified, then you may have some serious implications inside
[07:14] your business logic.
[07:15] So to handle these kind of scenarios, we can also use immutable objects. These immutable objects
[07:22] in other words, we can call them as data carrier classes.
[07:27] The reason why they are called as data carrier classes is, they primary purpose is to store the data
[07:33] and provide the methods to access the data. So how others can access the data inside an immutable object
[07:39] using the getter methods.
[07:41] But there is no way to change the data.
[07:43] That means this is going to act like a post card.
[07:46] Once someone returns something on the post card, it can be only be carried or sent over to other person
[07:53] and the other person
[07:54] he should be able to read the post card, and he will not be able to update any content inside the post
[08:00] card.

[08:05] Think like your frontend layer or frontend application.

[08:25] program, or if needed, the same data carrier object or immutable
[08:29] object can be transferred between multiple layers of the backend system.
[08:34] Inside backend system we are going to have multiple layers like controller layer, service layer,
[08:39] persistent layer or DB layer.
[08:41] To all these layers, we can try to send the same immutable object, and since it is an immutable object,
[08:47] we can happily sleep with an assumption that no one will be able to change the data inside this object.
[08:53] Now let's try to understand the differences between mutable and immutable objects very quickly.
[08:59] The very first difference between mutable and immutable objects is mutable objects requires synchronization
[09:06] whenever they are trying to be used inside a multithreading environment.
[09:11] So what is a synchronization?
[09:13] Synchronization is a process that developer has to implement that at a time
[09:18] a single thread can access a given object.
[09:21] If you don't implement the synchronization, then different threads inside your Java program.
[09:27] They will be able to manipulate the data inside mutable objects very easily.
[09:32] And with that you will end up race conditions.
[09:35] So what is a race condition?
[09:36] Race condition is a scenario where different threads have different set of data in their own hands.
[09:44] So one thread may have the designation as doctor, whereas other thread may have the designation of
[09:49] software engineer.
[09:50] And at the same time one more thread can come into picture and it can also try to manipulate the data.
[09:56] So with all these simultaneous manipulation of the data
[09:59] inside a mutable objects, it will result into the inconsistent state of your object.
[10:05] So that's why to overcome these kind of issues inside multi-threading environment synchronization has
[10:11] to be implemented.
[10:12] Whereas with immutable objects we don't have to worry about the synchronization, race conditions.
[10:18] Regardless of how many threads I have inside my program, all of them, they will be able to access
[10:24] the data inside these immutable objects without the need of synchronization.
[10:29] Since all threads they can only read the data.
[10:32] I don't have to worry much because no thread can change the data inside a immutable object.
[10:38] So that's why we can call these immutable objects as thread safe.
[10:41] So whenever you're trying to build a logic for multi-threading environment, you can consider the immutable objects.
[10:47] We are ready to discuss about
[10:49] what is a thread,
[10:50] what is multithreading inside Java ?
[10:52] This advanced topic we are going to discuss towards the end of the course.
[10:56] The next difference is mutable objects are going to provide more flexibility and they are going to be
[11:02] more efficient.
[11:03] The reason is once the object is created, the same object can be used multiple times by changing the
[11:11] data any number of times.
[11:13] Since we are not going to create the object from scratch with the new data, they are going to be efficient
[11:18] because already the object creation might have happened long back inside your program.
[11:24] But these mutable objects require careful handling to avoid issues related to concurrent access, especially
[11:32] in the multi threading environment.
[11:34] Whereas immutable objects may require more memory and potentially they may work slowly compared to the
[11:42] mutable objects.
[11:44] The reason is, every time you want to store new data, you need to create a fresh objects.
[11:49] And as you are trying to create more and more immutable objects, you're going to occupy more memory
[11:55] and it may potentially slow the performance of your application compared to the mutable objects.
[12:02] That's why most of the times Java developers, they will end up creating only the mutable objects.
[12:08] But if they have some special requirement where they don't want the object content not to be modified
[12:14] once the object is created in such scenarios, they are going to build the immutable objects.
[12:20] So the choice between mutable and immutable is always going to depend on the specific use case and the
[12:27] performance requirements of your application.
[12:30] I hope you are clear about mutable and immutable objects.

LECTURE: Autoboxing and unboxing - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, we are performing the boxing and unboxing manually with the help of the methods available
[00:06] inside the wrapper classes.
[00:08] For example, we are leveraging the valueOf() method to perform the boxing, whereas to perform the unboxing
[00:15] with the help of the wrapper objects, we are invoking the instance methods like intValue(), doubleValue(),
[00:21] and longValue().
[00:22] But here you may have a question which is boxing and unboxing seems to be a very most common scenario
[00:30] inside Java.
[00:31] Is there any better approach or is there any automated way of boxing and unboxing?
[00:36] It's a very great question and a valid question as well.
[00:39] When Java introduced the collections very first time Java team, they made these boxing and unboxing
[00:45] as manual process, which means that Java developers, they have to perform the boxing and unboxing
[00:52] manually with the help of these methods.
[00:54] But in the Java five version, the Java team, they made these boxing and unboxing automatic.
[01:02] So that's why from Java five there is a new concept came into picture which is auto boxing and auto
[01:08] unboxing.
[01:09] So let's try to understand how these boxing and unboxing is going to happen automatically.
[01:14] Like I said before, the Java is capable of performing automatic boxing and automatic unboxing from
[01:21] Java5 version.
[01:22] That's why these concept is commonly known as auto boxing and auto unboxing.
[01:28] First, let's try to understand how to perform the boxing automatically. Like you can see here,
[01:33] first, I have created the inter primitive data type variable with the name num and to the same variable
[01:39] I'm trying to assign the numerical value, which is 16.
[01:43] As a next step, I'm trying to assign this num variable directly to the object of Integer wrapper class.
[01:50] So this is auto boxing.
[01:51] So whenever I'm trying to assign a direct int literal value or a variable
[01:57] in such scenarios the boxing is going to happen automatically behind the scenes.
[02:02] We don't have to manually invoke the valueOf() method.
[02:05] So this is auto boxing.
[02:07] Whereas coming to the unboxing even this is also work very similarly.
[02:12] You can see first I'm trying to assign the 16 directly to the wrapper object of Integer.
[02:17] So at the very first line auto boxing is going to happen.
[02:21] Whereas in the second line I'm trying to assign these num object to the primitive data type variable
[02:28] which is num.
[02:29] So at the second line the unboxing is happening automatically.
[02:34] Did you see how easy it is with this auto boxing and unboxing?
[02:38] We never have to do the boxing or unboxing manually with the help of valueOf() method or intValue(), doubleValue().
[02:45] .
[02:46] or longValue() methods.
[02:47] We can use this auto boxing and unboxing feature only from the Java5 version.
[02:53] Do you know when Java five released?
[02:55] Java5 released a long back in 2004.
[02:58] In 2004, most of us might be in school, which means this feature is introduced long back, and right
[03:05] now we can happily use the auto boxing and unboxing without any manual code.
[03:11] Let's try to understand more details about auto boxing and unboxing these auto boxing and unboxing
[03:17] it is going to be performed when we compile the code.
[03:20] The JVM is completely clueless of the boxing and unboxing performed by the compiler, which means when
[03:27] we try to assign a primitive data type value to the wrapper class object, the auto boxing is going
[03:33] to happen behind the scenes.
[03:34] So by the time my JVM is trying to execute the bytecode of my Java program behind the scenes, the compiler
[03:41] will use the valueOf() method to convert that primitive data type value into the wrapper class object.
[03:47] The same applies for the unboxing as well.
[03:49] Here I want to share a very important note.
[03:52] So as of now everything seems to be good.
[03:55] Like you might be liking these auto boxing and unboxing a lot, but you need to be very careful whenever
[04:01] you're trying to use these auto boxing and and unboxing feature.
[04:05] While you are trying to deal with the null values. Like you can see here
[04:09] first, I have created an object of Integer wrapper class, and to the same I'm trying to assign the
[04:15] null value later on.
[04:17] If I try to assign this wrapper class object directly to the primitive data type variable, I'm going
[04:23] to get a NullPointerException.
[04:24] Do you know why?
[04:25] Because behind the scenes the compiler is going to write a code which is with the help of these n wrapper
[04:32] object
[04:32] it is going to invoke the intValue() method available inside the Integer wrapper class.
[04:38] So anything that we try to invoke on top of the null object, what do we get?
[04:43] We get our favorite exception which is NullPointerException.
[04:48] That's why whenever you are trying to deal with the wrapper objects that have null values, please do
[04:53] enough null checks and do enough unit testing to avoid these kind of surprises.
[04:58] I hope you are clear about the

LECTURE: [JAVA 7] Diamond Operator in Java
----------------------------------------

[00:00] As of now, whenever we are trying to create an collection object like ArrayList, we are trying to

[00:23] you can see if I try to hover on this, I'll be able to get that
[00:27] details of the warning, which is explicit type argument integer can be replaced with empty angle brackets.
[00:35] This means since we are already mentioning the element data type on the left hand side, while we are
[00:40] trying to declare the variable, we don't have to repeat the same information again on the right hand
[00:46] side.

[01:19] side.
[01:19] But whenever we are using the var data type, we should not delete what we have on the right hand side
[01:25] because we didn't mention anything about the element data type on the left hand side.
[01:30] That's why whenever you are trying to use a var keyword to declare and create an any Collection object,
[01:36] in those scenarios, you should mention the element data type on the right hand side.
[01:41] And at last here I can remove these String on the right hand side because on the left hand side I already
[01:47] mentioned, if you closely look at these empty angle bracket, it is looking like a diamond.
[01:53] That's why this operator is called as diamond operator.
[01:57] So whenever you are trying to use this syntax to declare any Collection object, it can be an
[02:03] ArrayList or it can be LinkedList or it can be Set implementation or Map implementation. Inside collections
[02:09] whenever you're following this syntax we call this kind of syntax is diamond operator syntax.
[02:16] And this diamond operator is only introduced from Java7.
[02:20] Before Java7, it is mandatory to mention the element data type both on the left hand side and
[02:26] the right hand side.
[02:27] Inside programming language there is a principle which is DRY,
[02:31] DRY means Don't Repeat Yourself by following these principle.
[02:37] This diamond operator is introduced in Java7.
[02:41] Since we are already mentioning the element data type on the left hand side, there is no need to mention
[02:45] on the right hand side.
[02:47] My recommendation is always use this diamond operator and don't try to mention the element data type
[02:52] on the right hand side unnecessarily.
[02:54] Whatever we discussed around the diamond operator I have mentioned in this slide for your reference,

LECTURE: ArrayList vs LinkedList

[00:00] Let's try to discuss about the differences between ArrayList and LinkedList.
[00:05] With this discussion, you should get a clarity under which scenarios you should use
[00:09] ArrayList and LinkedList.
[00:11] The very first difference is we know ArrayList is an implementation of List interface, and it is going
[00:17] to store the elements in an contiguous block of memory or contiguous memory locations.
[00:24] Since the elements are going to be stored in a contiguous memory location, accessing an element or
[00:30] reading an element is faster compared to the LinkedList.
[00:34] Coming to the story of the LinkedList, LinkedList is also an implementation class of List interface,
[00:41] but it is going to store all the elements as nodes with a reference to the next node and the previous
[00:47] node.
[00:48] Since LinkedList is going to store the elements with the help of nodes, it is going to allow faster
[00:54] insertion and deletion of elements from the middle of the LinkedList or from any index inside the LinkedList
[01:01] .

[01:02] The reason is very simple.
[01:04] The LinkedList has to update only the references of the affected nodes, whereas with the ArrayList
[01:10] all the subsequent elements, they are going to be affected and there needs to be moved either to the
[01:16] right hand side or to the left hand side to maintain that continuous memory location.
[01:21] The next difference is around the performance time whenever you are using the ArrayList, regardless
[01:26] of which index element you are trying to access, it can be 10,000 index elements or 1 million index
[01:33] element.
[01:34] You're always going to have a constant time off performance.

[01:43] then the same one millisecond time is also required to read any element.

[01:52] But coming to the LinkedList, whenever you are trying to perform the read operation, it is going
[01:57] to take the linear time, which is O(n), which means if the LinkedList is going to take one millisecond
[02:05] to read the very first element, and if you are trying to read the 10th index element, then your LinkedList
[02:10] is going to take one into ten milliseconds, which is ten milliseconds.

[02:21] also is going to increase.
[02:22] ArrayList

[02:29] especially from the middle of the List.

[02:37] from the middle of the List, or from any location inside your List object.

LECTURE: Subtype or Upper Bound Wildcards
----------------------------------------

[00:00] We had a very good discussion around what is a covariance and why it is not allowed inside collections.
[00:07] Whatever we discuss in the previous lecture around covariance, along with the examples, I have highlighted
[00:12] all of them inside these three slides.
[00:15] Now, as a next step, let's try to understand about one of the flavor inside generics. Which is subtype,
[00:22] or upper bound wild cards.
[00:24] Using these flavor of generic, we should be able to achieve covariance kind of functionality inside
[00:30] collections.
[00:31] So let's try to understand how to define these subtype or
[00:35] Upper bound wild cards.
[00:36] Whenever you are trying to define a generic inside your class or inside your method, you can follow
[00:42] these syntax which is question mark extends T.
[00:46] This means your class or your method
[00:48] it is only going to accept the elements which belongs to either T class or a child of T.
[00:56] Here T is a type used as the generics of collection.
[00:59] For example, you can see here I have a method with the name printEmployeeNames().
[01:04] To this method, we are trying to pass a Upper bound wild card or subtype generic after the collection
[01:11] name like ArrayList.
[01:12] I'm trying to mention question mark extends Employee.
[01:15] With this my method
[01:17] it is going to accept the ArrayList object, which is going to store either Employee objects or the
[01:23] subtypes of Employee like manager and developer.
[01:26] And inside this method we can write the generic code with the help of the superclass, which is Employee.
[01:32] The reason why this generic syntax is called as Upper bound wild cards is, with the help of this syntax,
[01:39] your method or your class at a max or at a upper bound
[01:43] it is going to accept only the Employee object, or it can accept the child elements.
[01:48] But you can't store or use the objects which are above the Employee inheritance hierarchy, like object
[01:55] or any other superclass.
[01:57] So we are trying to restrict the boundary up to a maximum of Employee.
[02:01] That's why this kind of syntax we can call it as upper bound or subtype wild card.
[02:07] Why this is called as subtype wild card.
[02:09] It is very simple,
[02:10] with this syntax, you are going to accept the subtypes of a given type that you have defined.
[02:15] So either the subtypes are allowed or the same data type objects also allowed. The question mark that
[02:21] we have inside the syntax like question mark extends Employee.
[02:24] It indicates some unknown subtype of Employee can be used inside this method or inside a class where
[02:32] you are going to use this syntax.
[02:33] So the question mark indicates wild card type, which is unknown.
[02:37] You can call this method with an Employee or an subtype like developer or manager.
[02:44] Whenever we are using this Upper bound wild card or subtype wild card inside our Java program, there
[02:50] is a restriction that you need to be aware.
[02:52] The restriction is we can't add a new element or object inside the collection.
[02:58] For example, here we have received a Collection object which is Employee and once this employees is
[03:04] received as an input to this method, inside this method or inside this for loop, I can't add a new
[03:09] element or object inside this class.
[03:12] The object can be belongs to employees or manager or developer.
[03:16] Still, I will not be able to make any changes to my Collection object.
[03:21] If you try to do the same, we are going to get a compilation error.
[03:23] We are going to see the demo in few seconds.
[03:25] The reason why we have this restriction inside collections is think for a second that we can add a element,
[03:32] or we can add an object whenever we are using these syntax.
[03:36] If adding an element is allowed, it may result into an heap
[03:40] pollution.
[03:41] There is a concept of Heap pollution inside Java.
[03:43] What is going to happen is think like your method received an ArrayList object which is capable of
[03:48] storing the subtype of employee like Manager.
[03:52] In such scenarios, it is not going to make sense to allow to add a developer object into the ArrayList
[03:58] of manager, because they both are different subtypes and they are independent on each other,
[04:03] and there is no direct relationship between them.
[04:06] To avoid these kind of heap pollution scenarios, adding an element whenever you are using the upper
[04:12] bound wild card or subtype wild card is not allowed.
[04:16] I hope this makes sense to you.
[04:17] Let's see the demo of these Upper bound wild cards inside IntelliJ.

[05:09] With this Upper bound wild card syntax.
[05:12] Now my method is capable of accepting an ArrayList object that can store Employee objects or its subtype

LECTURE: [JAVA 8] HashMap improvements in Java 8
----------------------------------------

[00:00] In the last two lectures, when we were trying to discuss about the internal working of the HashMap,
[00:05] I told you that whenever an hash collision happens, it is going to store the entries in a LinkedList
[00:12] format.
[00:13] But it is partially true because there are some enhancements or improvements introduced as part of the
[00:21] Java 8.
[00:22] So let's try to understand what are these improvements that are introduced inside the HashMap as part
[00:27] of Java 8.
[00:28] Inside Java 8, HashMap was improved to include a new data structure called TreeNodes.
[00:35] This was done to improve the performance in cases where HashMap contains a large number of entries with
[00:43] the same hash code, causing the hash collisions and the creation of long LinkedList.
[00:49] We know based upon our previous discussion, whenever the hash collision has happened, the new entry
[00:53] is going to be appended as an node to the existing LinkedList.
[00:58] If the HashMap, it is going to keep on adding more and more elements or nodes to the same LinkedList
[01:04] inside the same bucket.
[01:06] When you are trying to read the value based upon a given key, it is going to be slow because we know
[01:11] inside LinkedList the reading operation is going to be very slow.
[01:16] Think like there is a value present at the 11th node, but in order to read that 11th node value, the
[01:23] reading operation has to start from right from the very first node inside the LinkedList.
[01:28] So to overcome these kind of challenges, a new data structure which is tree nodes is introduced as
[01:35] part of Java 8.
[01:36] But this doesn't mean from Java 8 we are always going to store the elements in a TreeNode format.
[01:43] Whenever a hash collision happen, it is not going to work.
[01:46] HashMap is always going to start with the LinkedList data structure.
[01:50] When a number of nodes inside a LinkedList exceeds a configured number inside the JDK library, then
[01:57] that entire LinkedList data structure is going to be converted into a TreeNode format.
[02:03] Let's try to understand more details about this TreeNodes.
[02:07] They work by creating a self-balancing binary tree within the same bucket.
[02:12] When you are trying to add new entries to the same bucket, the tree is restructured as needed to maintain
[02:19] the balance and ensure that retrieval time always remains fast.
[02:24] How it is going to be fast.
[02:25] I'm going to explain you in few seconds.
