LECTURE: List vs Set
----------------------------------------

[00:00] One of the important question that you may face inside your Java interviews is, people may ask you to
[00:07] explain you about the differences between List and Set, and under which scenarios
[00:12] you need to choose one of them.
[00:13] To answer these kind of questions, you should have a good clarity about the differences between List
[00:18] and Set.
[00:19] That's why inside this lecture, let's put few minutes efforts to understand the differences between
[00:24] the List and Set.
[00:25] We know both List and Set are the interfaces inside the Java collection framework.
[00:30] However, there are good amount of differences between them.
[00:33] The very first difference is List can contain duplicate elements.
[00:37] If you have a requirement to maintain a collection of elements that can contain duplicates, you need
[00:43] to use a List.
[00:44] Whereas if you are looking for an option which will not allow the duplicates, then in that scenario
[00:49] you can happily use Set and its implementation classes.
[00:53] The next difference is around the order of insertion.
[00:57] By default List
[00:58] always maintain the order of insertion while Set.
[01:01] They do not maintain.
[01:03] If the order of insertion is important to you, always prefer List.
[01:08] The Set does not maintain the order of insertion by default.
[01:11] If you are looking for the order of insertion within the Set implementations, then you need to go for
[01:17] the LinkedHashSet.
[01:18] The third difference between List and Set is, List allows for positional access to elements, which means
[01:25] we have 1000 elements inside your List.
[01:27] You should be able to easily pick 200 element or 300 element, or 250 element without any performance
[01:35] issues, because we know by default List is going to maintain the elements in an sequential memory.
[01:40] Locations coming to the Set,
[01:43] Set does not going to provide the positional access.
[01:46] Instead, you can quickly check if an element is present inside a Set or not with the help of contains()
[01:54] method.
[01:54] Off course, List also have contains() method, but whenever you are using contains method on top of a
[02:00] List object, it is going to iterate all the elements one by one, whereas in the scenario of Set it
[02:06] is going to be very quick.
[02:08] It is going to calculate the hash code of your element and pick the corresponding bucket number inside
[02:13] the HashMap, and straight away will return you whether a given element is present or not.
[02:18] Moving on to the next difference list generally have better performance than sets for positional access.
[02:24] This is because List use an index to access the elements, which is faster than checking every element
[02:31] in a Set for membership.
[02:33] This means if you are looking for an option to randomly access the elements with the help of index,
[02:39] always prefer list because they are going to have better performance, whereas on the other side sets
[02:45] they are going to have better performance than List for testing the membership.

[00:47] given priority.

LECTURE: Advantages of Enums
----------------------------------------

[00:00] By this time, it should be pretty clear for you that enums are the clear winner compared to the traditional
[00:07] Java constants.
[00:09] Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss about the advantages of enums so that it is going to help
[00:15] you inside your Java interviews.
[00:16] Because inside Java interviews, many times people may ask you, why should we use enums when we can
[00:22] achieve the same job with the help of Java constants?
[00:26] That's why let's try to understand the advantages one by one, the very first, and a major advantage
[00:31] that we are going to get with the help of enums is type safety.
[00:35] Enums provide type safety by allowing developers to define a fixed set of named values.
[00:41] So this will stop other developers to use invalid values or wrong data types as an input to the business
[00:49] logic, like we saw in the previous lectures demo.
[00:52] Whenever we are using enum as an input parameter, other developers, they will be able to invoke my
[00:58] method only if they are passing a valid value of enum.
[01:02] The second advantage is around the readability.
[01:04] Enum makes our code more readable by providing a clear and concise way to represent a fixed set of related
[01:12] constants.
[01:13] I saw many projects in my career where they are not using enums.
[01:17] What they are going to do is, they are going to put thousands of constants inside a single Java file,
[01:22] and it is going to make developers life tough.
[01:25] Whenever someone is looking for a particular scenario constant, they need to end up searching that
[01:31] entire file.
[01:32] And sometimes they may have constants with very similar names as well.
[01:37] Whereas with enums we can build multiple enum data types which are going to hold the constants based
[01:43] upon a particular scenario.
[01:44] For example, if someone is looking for the constants which are related to the task priority, they
[01:50] can find all the constants related to the task priority inside the PriorityEnum class.
[01:55] As a standard, we know developers
[01:57] they are not going to maintain other scenario constants inside the PriorityEnum class.
[02:02] So that's why using enums is always going to improve the readability of your code.
[02:07] The next advantage is around the robustness enums.
[02:10] They are going to make your code more robust by providing a centralized and consistent way to handle
[02:17] a set of related constants.
[02:19] If the help of enums, we are going to make our life easy to modify the code in future without introducing
[02:26] bugs.
[02:26] So whenever I want to introduce a new constant, or whenever I want to change a value of my constant
[02:32] or date of my enum constant, the change is always going to be in a single place.
[02:37] We don't have to worry about compiling the multiple dependent files.
[02:41] After robustness, we have the advantage around the code organization.
[02:45] Like we discussed previously.
[02:46] With the help of enums, we can group related constants together in a particular file.
[02:52] In all the previous lecture, we have created so many enum classes one to store the priority related
[02:57] constants, other to store the day related constants, and the other one related to the size related
[03:03] constants.
[03:03] So whenever you are following enums, you will end up organizing your code and constants based upon
[03:09] your scenario.
[03:10] And the last advantage is around the switch statements we saw in the previous lectures
[03:14] how easily we can use the enums along with the switch statements or switch expressions.
[03:20] By combining both enum and switch blocks, we can write business logic to handle a set of related cases.
[03:27] So these are the advantages on using the enums.
[03:30] So my humble request always is to implement the constant logic with the help of enums wherever possible.

LECTURE: Primitive Type functional interfaces - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Inside this lecture, let's try to discuss about the last set of functional interfaces, which are primitive
[00:06] type functional interfaces.
[00:08] So what are these interfaces?
[00:10] What is the purpose of them.
[00:11] This might be your question.
[00:12] So let's try to understand the same.
[00:14] All the functional interfaces that we have discussed so far like predicate function, consumer or by
[00:19] functional interfaces, they are going to accept or return only the object type values like integer,
[00:26] double, float and long.
[00:28] So these are all the wrapper class representation of the primitive data types.
[00:32] If you have a scenario where you want to build a lambda expression with the help of these function interfaces
[00:38] like predicate function consumer, which is going to accept the primitive data type values, then you're
[00:44] going to have a serious performance problem, because whenever we pass a primitive input value like
[00:50] int long double float behind the scenes, Java is going to perform the auto boxing where it is going
[00:56] to convert this primitive data type to the wrapper objects.
[00:59] And similarly, once the logic is being executed, Java has to convert them back to the primitive types
[01:05] using unboxing.
[01:07] So think like you have implemented a lambda expression with the help of function interface.
[01:13] So this function interface, it's supposed to accept the int value as an input and post that inside
[01:19] the business logic, the lambda expression, it is going to multiply it with the two and return the
[01:25] new value as an output.
[01:27] So in this scenario, it is pretty simple that we are dealing with the inter primitive value.
[01:31] But we know the drawback with the function is it is only going to accept the input and return the output
[01:37] in the form of integer wrapper object.
[01:40] That's why behind the scenes all these autoboxing and unboxing is going to happen.
[01:45] Since there is going to be lot of autoboxing and unboxing is going to happen, it may impact performance,
[01:52] especially in the scenarios where you're trying to feed your lambda expression for the millions of elements
[01:58] present inside a stream or a collection.
[02:01] So in those kind of scenarios, you will see a performance issue if you leverage the function interfaces
[02:08] that we have discussed so far.
[02:09] That's why whenever you have a scenario where you are dealing with the primitive data type values as
[02:14] an input or output, in all such scenarios, you can use the primitive type of functional interfaces.
[02:20] There are good amount of interfaces under this category.
[02:24] So let's try to understand what are those.
[02:26] You can see the very first function interface that we have is inter predicate.
[02:30] We know the return type from the predicate is always boolean.
[02:34] So they should not be any confusion around this.
[02:36] But coming to the input parameter, if you have a scenario where you want to accept the input value
[02:43] with the primitive data type int.
[02:45] In such scenarios, you can use the inter predicate to build the lambda expression.
[02:51] Similarly, if you are looking for a double as an input parameter, you can leverage the double predicate
[02:57] followed by long predicate.
[02:58] If you have a scenario where you want to accept the long as an input value, let me show you one of
[03:04] these predicate functional interfaces inside Intellige.
[03:08] Here I'm going to search for inter predicate.
[03:11] If I can open.
[03:12] You can see this time it is accepting the input parameter as primitive data type, which is int.
[03:18] With that there won't be any auto boxing required.
[03:22] Whereas if you look for the normal predicate interface, it is going to accept the input in the form
[03:29] of object.
[03:30] So that's why we will be forced to mention integer wrapper class whenever we are trying to define a
[03:36] lambda expression with the help of this predicate.
[03:38] But if you know that you're going to accept the inter primitive data type as an input, please use this
[03:44] int predicate or double predicate or long predicate based upon your requirements.
[03:49] After predicate, we have function related functional interfaces.
[03:53] So you can see here we have a function interface with the name into function.
[03:57] If you are working on a scenario where your function has to accept the inter primitive value as an input,
[04:03] and the return type can be any object data type.
[04:06] In such scenarios, you can use these inter function.
[04:09] In the similar lines we have double function long function, which is going to accept double and long
[04:15] as an input values, but the return type can be defined based upon.

[00:00] As of now

[00:21] And with that, you may receive a lot of compilation errors.
[00:24] To resolve these kind of compilation issues.
[00:26] First, you need to understand how the variable scope is going to work inside the lambda expression.
[00:32] So let's try to understand more details about scoping concept inside the lambda expressions.
[00:38] Like
[00:38] we know there is a similarity between the lambda expression and the method declarations like they both
[00:43] accept the input parameter and they both are going to have body which can be written inside the curly
[00:48] braces.

[00:55] to accept first.

[01:01] similarly inside the normal methods and the lambda expressions.

[01:11] it is not going to create its own scope.

LECTURE: Finding and Matching methods in Streams
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Streams
[00:01] API has some terminal operation methods, which is going to help you to find an particular element or
[00:07] to match a particular element.
[00:09] So these methods we call them as finding and matching methods.
[00:14] Under this category there are five different types of terminal operations or terminal methods are available.
[00:21] So these methods are allMatch(), anyMatch(), noneMatch(), findAny() and findFirst().
[00:27] I'm going to discuss in detail about all these methods by providing examples.
[00:32] But before I try to show you the demo, let me introduce about this method on a high level.
[00:37] So the very first method which is allMatch(), it is going to boolean value true as an output in the
[00:42] scenarios, if all your elements inside your stream are matched with the predicate condition that you
[00:49] have provided. But coming to the anyMatch(), it is going to give the output as true
[00:53] even if one of the element inside your stream is matching with the predicate condition and noneMatch(),
[01:00] it is going to give the output as true.
[01:02] If none of your elements inside your stream, they are matching with the predicate condition.
[01:08] And at last we have two methods which are going to help us to find an element.
[01:12] So findAny() will find any of the element that matches to your condition.
[01:18] Whereas the findFirst() method, it is going to give the first element present inside your stream that
[01:25] you built based upon some intermediate operation or based upon some business logic.
[01:30] The beauty of all these methods are they are going to work just like how we have logical and and logical
[01:36] or operations.
[01:37] What do I mean by they're going to work very similar to short circuiting operations.
[01:42] We have certain short circuiting operations like Logical AND and Logical OR when we are discussing
[01:48] about these logical operators.
[01:50] I told you that when you are trying to apply and operator based upon two different operands, if the
[01:57] first operand gives the output as false, then your Logical And operator, it is not going to evaluate
[02:03] the second operand because there is no need of evaluating the second element if the first operand itself
[02:09] is giving the output as false.
[02:11] Very similarly, in the Logical OR operation, if the very first element is giving the output as true,
[02:17] then it is never going to evaluate the second operand, because in the scenario of our condition, even
[02:23] if one of the operand is true, then the overall output is going to be true.
[02:27] So the same strategy here also these methods are going to follow especially like allMatch() and anyMatch().
[02:34] So allMatch()
[02:35] what it is going to do is, whenever it find an element which is not matching with your predicate condition,
[02:41] then immediately it is going to return the output as false.
[02:44] It is not going to evaluate the predicate condition on all the elements. In the similar lines,
[02:49] anyMatch() also
[02:50] it is going to give the output as true as soon as it identify a first element which matches to
[02:58] your predicate condition.
[03:00] The same principle applies to the other methods like findAny() and findFirst().
[03:04] So both these methods are going to return an element from your stream.
[03:10] In the scenario of findFirst(), it is going to be the first element and all the remaining elements.
[03:14] It is not going to look and bother about them.
[03:16] And similarly, inside the findAny(), it is going to randomly pick one of the element, and it is also
[03:23] not going to bother about all the remaining elements.

LECTURE: Collections Vs Streams
----------------------------------------

[00:00] We almost covered all the details around the stream API.
[00:03] We discussed everything around the intermediate operations, terminal operations, parallel processing.
[00:09] So now we have a very good understanding around the stream API and how to process the elements inside
[00:14] a collection with the help of streams and the lambda expressions.
[00:18] As part of this lecture, let's try to understand what are the differences between collections and streams.
[00:23] We know collections are present inside Java from day one, whereas streams they are introduced as part
[00:29] of Java 8.
[00:30] So this is one of the famous interviews around the Java Collections and Streams API.
[00:35] That's why let's try to put some efforts understanding the differences between the collections and streams.
[00:41] The very first and most important difference between collections and stream is, collections
[00:45] they are going to hold the elements inside the memory or inside the heap memory, whereas streams,
[00:53] they are not going to store the elements inside any memory, all the elements, they are going to be
[00:58] stored using the underlying collection data source.
[01:01] We already discussed in detail about this point in the previous lectures.
[01:05] Moving on to the next difference, a collection is going to be eagerly constructed and the elements
[01:12] can be added or removed.
[01:14] So whenever we are trying to build a collection object and try to add all the elements inside each,
[01:20] these operation is going to be done eagerly.
[01:23] That means before you try to perform any operations on top of your collection object, all the elements
[01:29] might have stored inside a heap memory, but coming to the stream, they are going to operate lazily.
[01:35] For example, if you are trying to run a map() operation with the help of Stream object, it is not going
[01:40] to load all the hundreds of elements inside your underlying collection data source.
[01:45] Instead, it is going to read the element lazily one by one.
[01:50] The next difference is pretty easy collections.
[01:53] They don't use any functional interfaces and lambda expressions, but on the other side streams they
[01:58] are going to use lot of functional interfaces along with the lambda expressions.
[02:03] We can't imagine streams API without lambda expressions and functional interfaces.
[02:09] The next difference is collections are non consumable.
[02:12] That means collections can be traversed to multiple times without creating again.
[02:18] If you have a List of object, you can try to iterate it any number of times with the multiple
[02:24] for loops and while loops, you're not going to get any exception.
[02:28] But on the other side, streams are consumable, which means you can only traverse them once if you
[02:34] want to traverse or iterate the elements inside stream one more time, the only option that you have
[02:39] is to create the stream one more time.
[02:42] If you try to traverse the same Stream object multiple times, like we discussed in the previous lectures,
[02:47] we are going to get an IllegalStateException.
[02:50] Coming to the last difference, it says collections are iterated using external loop like for loop and
[02:57] while loop only.
[02:58] So whenever we are dealing with the collections, we need to give low level instructions to the JRE
[03:03] or the Java and how to iterate the elements inside a collection.
[03:07] Whereas with streams we don't have to give any low level instructions, we can follow the functional
[03:12] style of programming as long as we are using intermediate operations or terminal operations to process
[03:18] the elements inside stream, the iteration responsibility is going to be taken care by the Java
[03:24] internally.
[03:25] We as a developers, we don't have to manually iterate the stream elements.
[03:29] So these are the differences between collections and streams.
[03:32] I hope you are clear.
[03:34] Thank you and I'll catch you in the next lecture, bye.

[01:36] In all those scenarios you can happily use the join() method.
[01:40] I hope this is clear.
[01:41] Moving on to the next set of methods which are setPriority() and getPriority().
[01:46] We know JVM and operating system and CPU cores
[01:51] they are capable of processing multiple threads many times will try to execute our Java program with
[01:57] multiple threads.
[01:58] So if you're trying to feed a multiple threads to your operating system or to your JVM or to the CPU
[02:04] cores, sometimes we may want to tell to the JVM or operating system that I want a specific thread to
[02:12] give some more priority, so that the logic associated to it is going to be executed sooner than expected.
[02:19] So in all such scenarios, we can leverage these priority related methods.
[02:23] By default, each thread that you're going to create, it is going to have the normal priority, which
[02:29] is indicated by the int value five.
[02:32] Like I highlighted here in Java programming language, a thread's priority is represented by an integer
[02:37] within the range of 1 to 10.
[02:39] So one indicates minimum priority and the maximum priority is indicated by ten.
[02:45] So whenever you are using the setPriority() method, we can only pass the int values right from 1 to
[02:52] 10, and by default each thread.
[02:54] When it is going to get created, it is going to have the priority as five, which means it is going
[03:00] to have a normal priority.
[03:01] But here you need to make a very important note, which is think like
[03:06] as a developer, I'm very greedy and I'm trying to mark all my threads as highest priority with the
[03:12] value ten with that operating system or JVM, they are never going to always give priority to my highest
[03:19] priority threads.
[03:19] Only behind the scenes operating system also will do its own due diligence.
[03:24] It will make sure that no thread starvation scenario is happening.
[03:29] So what is a thread starvation scenario?
[03:31] Think like someone is trying to execute a program with the lowest priority threads, and the other developer
[03:36] is trying to execute the program with the highest priority threads.
[03:39] So in this kind of scenario, operating system is not going to give priority only to the highest priority
[03:45] threads.
[03:46] It will make sure even the lowest priority threads, they are getting enough CPU time.
[03:51] Otherwise the lowest priority threads always they are going to keep on waiting and that will result
[03:56] into the thread starvation scenario.
[03:59] That's why don't be under the assumption since you marked your thread as highest priority, it is not
[04:04] guaranteed that the JVM or operating system is going to execute your thread on priority.
[04:09] We can only let JVM or operating system know that my thread has highest priority, and it's up to the
[04:16] operating system or JVM on how to handle it.
[04:20] And in the scenarios where two threads have the same priority, then JVM or operating system, they
[04:26] are going to execute the threads in the Fifo order.
[04:29] So what is Fifo order First In First Out order?

LECTURE: Introduction to Race condition & synchronized keyword
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Building a Java program with the help of multithreading concept is somewhat complex compared to normal
[00:06] Java program.
[00:07] The reason is very obvious when multiple threads they are trying to execute your business logic parallely.
[00:13] You may need to handle lot many conditions or lot many complexities that your program may face at runtime.
[00:21] One such important complexity is race condition.
[00:25] So whenever you are dealing with the multiple threads, your program may have a race condition.
[00:32] So first let's try to understand what is this race condition.
[00:35] And later on we can try to understand how to handle these race condition.
[00:39] The race condition happens when two threads which are trying to access a shared variable at the same
[00:47] time.
[00:47] So both these threads like first thread and the second thread, they read the same value from the variable.
[00:52] But at later point of time when these threads, they want to update the same shared variable
[00:58] then a race condition will happen.
[01:01] Think like when both these threads they are trying to update the shared variable at the same time.
[01:06] They will be racing with each other to see which thread is going to write the latest value into the
[01:13] shared variable.
[01:14] So the value of the thread that writes its value at the end is going to be preserved.
[01:19] For example, think like
[01:21] initially the shared variable has a value as zero at later point of time.
[01:26] The same shared value is going to be updated by the thread one to the number ten.
[01:31] Here in the race condition, the thread one wins because it is able to first update the value inside
[01:38] the shared variable, though it wins the race, but its value is going to be overrided by the other thread,
[01:44] because thread two is going to overwrite the value present inside the shared variable with the new value
[01:51] at a later point of time.
[01:52] So this is a race condition.
[01:54] Let me give you an example so that it is going to make more sense to you.
[01:58] Like you can see here, I have a map with the name reserved tables.
[02:02] So inside this map think like we are going to store the table name as a key.
[02:08] And who reserved that table as a value.
[02:11] Think like this Java program that I'm showing right now
[02:14] it is going to be executed in some restaurant web application.
[02:18] So the restaurant has a booking functionality inside their web application.
[02:23] There is a very good chance that two multiple users may try to book the same table at the same point
[02:30] of time.
[02:31] So in these kind of scenarios, what is going to happen is thread one.
[02:35] It is going to check if these reserved table map contains the key table one.
[02:40] So indirectly it is checking if there is any one reserved that table one.
[02:44] Since these reserved table initially it is an empty map.
[02:48] So this condition inside the if condition it is going to give false.
[02:52] If we apply the Not condition on top of the false, the overall condition of this if condition is going
[02:57] to become true and the logic present inside this if block is going to be executed at the same time behind
[03:03] the scenes.
[03:04] Thread 2
[03:04] also, it is going to run the same logic.
[03:08] It is checking whether the reserved tables contains that table one as a key, since initially it read
[03:15] the reserved table which is an empty here
[03:18] also, this if condition is going to be executed and this thread 2
[03:22] also it is going to update the table one with the user two.
[03:25] So if you see here both these thread 1 and thread 2, they try to update the same shared variable
[03:31] at the same point of time with just a few fraction of seconds difference.
[03:36] In this scenario, let's assume the thread one wins the race and it wrote the value which is user one
[03:42] to this table.
[03:43] And with that the user one
[03:45] he is going to get a message inside the website saying that hey, congratulations, you reserved that
[03:49] table one.
[03:50] And with that message, the end user will be under the assumption his reservation is completed successfully.
[03:56] But behind the scenes, what happened just after few fraction of seconds?
[04:00] The thread 2 it tried to overwrite the reservation with the new user, which is user 2.
[04:06] So with this logic, if both these user one and user two go to the restaurant at the given time, only
[04:13] the user two will be able to get the table 1 because the user one data is overriding by the thread 2
[04:19] .
[04:20] So this is one of the serious problem that you may face while you are trying to implement a logic with
[04:25] the help of multi-threading environment.
[04:27] The problem here we have is, there is a shared variable which is the reserved tables HashMap.
[04:33] Both these threads are trying to update these reserved table at the same time.
[04:37] When they are trying to update the variable at the same time, obviously they both will not be able
[04:42] to write at the same time, just with a fraction of seconds difference.
[04:46] Both of these threads, they are going to write their values and whatever thread committed the value
[04:51] at the end, its value is going to be maintained inside the shared variable.
[04:56] So how to resolve this race condition?
[04:58] It's very simple
[04:59] we
[05:00] need to take the help of synchronized keyword like we discussed briefly in the previous lecture.
[05:05] Synchronized keyword is used to control the access of multiple threads to the shared resources.
[05:12] So whenever we are using this keyword, it is going to ensure that only one thread can execute a synchronized
[05:19] block or a method at a time.
[05:21] So the synchronized keyword can be used in two forms.
[05:24] You can use the synchronized keyword along with the block of code.
[05:28] Whenever you have some complex logic which needs to be executed by only one thread at a time.
[05:34] In such scenarios, you are going to keep all such complex logic inside the curly braces.
[05:39] And just before this curly braces, you're going to mention the synchronized keyword along with the
[05:44] shared object that you're trying to write.
[05:47] So with that, this synchronized block ensures that only one thread at a time can execute the code within
[05:53] the block.
[05:53] So if you try to apply the same synchronized keyword logic with the previous example, what we have
[05:59] to do is we need to keep these shared variable logic inside the synchronized block.
[06:05] And with that, only a one thread will be able to read and overwrite at a time while the thread1
[06:11] is doing the reading and writing operation on the shared object, the thread2
[06:16] it is going to keep waiting as soon as the thread1 completes the execution of this synchronized block,
[06:22] then thread2 will enter into the synchronized block.
[06:25] So this is how it is going to work.
[06:27] So we need to use the synchronized block.
[06:29] Whenever you have some piece of code which needs to be executed by one thread at a time.
[06:34] In the similar lines, you can also apply the synchronized keyword on top of a method itself.
[06:40] If you want your entire method to be executed only one thread at a time, then you can mention the synchronized
[06:47] keyword
[06:47] just before the return type of your method.
[06:50] You can use the synchronized keyword on top of the static methods and on top of instance methods.
[06:54] So whenever a method is declared as synchronized, it implicitly uses the Object instance at the class
[07:01] object as a monitor.
[07:02] I hope you are clear with this.
[07:04] I also mentioned a picture here, saying that threads are going to wait for their chance to execute
[07:09] this method, or to execute these block.
[07:12] This way we can avoid the conditions like race conditions.

LECTURE: [JAVA 21] Introduction to Virtual Threads - Part 1

[00:00] The latest buzzword in Java multithreading concept is virtual threads.

[00:15] These virtual threads are going to be a game changer for all the applications where they are using lot
[00:23] many threads as part of their business logic.
[00:26] As of now, we're just trying to create an object of Thread class and using the same.
[00:30] We are trying to invoke the start() method join() method.

[00:45] The answer is very simple.
[00:46] Virtual threads are lightweight in nature.
[00:49] With that, you can create millions of virtual threads inside your Java program.
[00:56] There won't be any restriction, whereas with a normal thread, since they are not lightweight like
[01:01] virtual threads, you will be limited with how many threads you can create inside your application based
[01:07] upon your Ram, memory and CPU cores.
[01:10] Oracle team
[01:11] they are working on these virtual threads from many years under the project name Loom.
[01:16] So Loom is a Oracle's initiative aimed at tackling the complexities associated with the developing,
[01:23] maintaining and monitoring high throughput concurrent applications.
[01:28] Finally, after doing a lot of research and testing, virtual threads are introduced in Java 21.
[01:35] So to understand in detail about what is a virtual thread and how it is different from a normal thread,
[01:40] first we need to understand some basics of operating system and threads.
[01:44] So let's try to understand the same. Inside operating system
[01:48] there are two types of threads that you can create.
[01:52] The very first type is kernel threads.
[01:55] So these threads in other words we can call them as operating system threads.
[02:00] These kernel threads are OS threads
[02:02] they are going to be overseen and scheduled by the operating system kernel.
[02:06] These threads are relatively heavyweight in terms of resources and requires system calls for their creation,
[02:14] scheduling and synchronization.
[02:16] So these kernel threads, they are going to be created strictly for the operating system purpose.
[02:21] That's why whenever you try to start your operating system like Windows or Mac, it is going to take
[02:27] some 30s or one minute based upon your computer and operating system.
[02:32] So during all these 30s or one minute behind the scenes, your operating system taking enough time to
[02:38] boot up and create all these kernel threads.
[02:41] The other type of threads are user level threads.
[02:45] So what are user level threads?
[02:46] If you try to run any software, or if you try to execute any program like Java
[02:51] so these softwares are Java programs
[02:53] they can be able to create the threads.
[02:56] All such threads we can call them as user threads.
[02:59] Throughout this section we are able to create the threads inside a Java program with the help of Thread
[03:04] class.
[03:04] So all these threads, we can call them as user threads, because a particular library or a particular
[03:10] software is trying to create these threads, but not the operating system.
[03:14] Compared to the kernel threads, the user threads are lightweight in nature, and creating and destroying
[03:20] these user threads is faster compared to the OS threads.

LECTURE: [JAVA 24] Finisher in a Stream Gatherer
----------------------------------------

[00:00] The next component of stream gatherers that we're going to focus is Finisher.
[00:05] Providing this Finisher is also optional, just like Initializer.
[00:09] But there are certain scenarios where you should definitely provide Finisher.
[00:13] Let's try to understand what are those scenarios and what is the purpose of this Finisher.
[00:18] As I said before, the Finisher is an optional part of a Gatherer that is called after all elements
[00:25] have been processed by the stream.
[00:28] Whatever logic that you're going to define inside the Finisher.
[00:31] It is only going to be executed once. Even if your Gatherer is trying to process 1 million input elements
[00:37] from the upstream.
[00:39] Still, the logic inside the Finisher is going to be executed only once.
[00:43] With the help of this Finisher, we can Flush out any remaining data from the mutable state.
[00:49] It is also useful when your buffer elements using a greedy integrator.
[00:54] We're going to discuss about these greedy integrator in a few minutes.
[00:57] Finishers can also be used in the scenarios where the final output depends on the end of the stream
[01:04] logic.
[01:04] When is this Finisher is going to be called ? after the stream is done
[01:08] consuming elements.
[01:09] When I say the stream, the intermediate operation that you are going to develop with the help of Gatherer.
[01:15] Once it process all the elements, then only this finisher logic is going to be executed once per entire
[01:23] stream run.
[01:23] Using finisher, we can emit anything left inside the memory or state that was not yet pushed to the
[01:29] downstream.
[01:30] I know you may have too many questions around the finisher.
[01:33] That's why I'm going to show you an example, which is going to clear all your doubts.
[01:37] The main objective of this program is when I receive an input like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5,
[01:43] 6, 7 inside the output, I want to batch the elements with a size of 3.
[01:48] As you can see here, my output is a list.
[01:51] Inside that list I have inner list as well.
[01:53] The very first list it is having 3 elements by batching the first 3 element values, followed
[01:59] by the next list batches the next 3 elements.
[02:03] Any leftover elements like these 7.
[02:05] We should also push them into the output.
[02:08] This kind of complex requirements can be easily achieved with the help of finisher.

[00:00] So far we discussed the basic concepts of gatherers API.
[00:04] As a next step, let's try to understand how to build the Parallel Gatherers.
[00:09] In the same process, we're also going to explore about the combiner optional component that we can
[00:14] provide while we are building an intermediate operation with the help of Gatherers API.
[00:19] By using Parallel Gatherers, we should be able to process our elements inside our intermediate operation
[00:27] in multiple threads.
[00:29] Java provides different ways to define parallel gatherers depending on whether we want to use internal
[00:35] state inside our business logic.
[00:38] If you're not using any internal state inside your business logic, then building parallel gatherers
[00:44] is very simple.
[00:44] Otherwise, you need to take care of merging all the internal mutable states that you are receiving
[00:51] from multiple threads before pushing the output to the downstream.
[00:55] On a high level, there are three different flavors that we can use to build the parallel gatherers.
[01:00] The very first flavor is ,when you are invoking the of() factory method of gatherer.
[01:05] If you are passing only the integrator logic, then all the elements from the upstream, they are going
[01:11] to be processed parallelly by executing your intermediate operator logic.
[01:16] When you are using this flavor, it means you don't want to use any mutable state inside your business
[01:22] logic,
[01:22] there won't be any finisher and this kind of parallel gathers,
[01:25] they are simple and safe for parallel execution.
[01:28] Whatever logic that you are going to define inside your integrator, the same logic will be executed
[01:33] parallelly for all the elements that is being received from the upstream.

[01:51] otherwise don't push the same.

[02:04] We already saw the demo of this flavor,
[02:06] please remember always the thumb rule is if you are using the of() factory method from the Gatherer interface
[02:12] behind the scenes, the gatherer logic is going to be executed parallelly by using multiple threads.
[02:19] In case if your business logic does not support parallel processing, and if you want to make sure to
[02:24] run the logic sequentially one by one.

[02:33] Let's move on to the second flavor,
[02:34] the second flavor is,
[02:36] along with the integrator.

[02:46] the elements parallelly.

LECTURE: [JAVA 24] Interrupting and Chaining Gatherers
----------------------------------------

[00:00] When we are processing data with the help of Gatherer API. It is also going to give an flexibility
[00:07] or an option to the developer to interrupt the stream processing whenever developer wanted,
[00:13] based upon certain business logic.We know that the integrator logic that we are going to define at
[00:18] the end of the day, it has to return a boolean. Based upon these boolean that we are trying to return
[00:24] from our intermediate operation.
[00:25] The upstream is going to decide whether to send the next value or not for the intermediate operation.
[00:32] We already saw a demo previously where when I'm trying to return a false, the upstream is not sending
[00:37] any new values.
[00:38] That is one option of interrupting a stream when you are processing the data with the help of Gatherer
[00:43] API, based upon your business logic,

[00:23] So what are scope to values?
[00:25] By using the scope to values, we should be able to share immutable data between a method and its colleagues
[00:34] without explicitly passing that data as method parameters.
[00:38] We know inside Java, a thread is responsible to handle a request, and as part of the request business
[00:44] logic, multiple methods will be executed.
[00:47] When a thread is calling a method like M1, this m1 may call other method like m2 from m2, it may call
[00:54] to M3 and this way in real enterprise applications are inside framework code, a good amount of methods
[01:02] will be called internally from one method to other method.
[01:05] So if you have a scenario where you want to share the data in between these methods, like if I want
[01:11] to share the data from these M1 to M4.
[01:14] We have various options inside Java.
[01:17] These scope to values is a modern approach to share the data between the methods without explicitly
[01:23] passing as a method parameters.
[01:25] We're going to explore more details around this.
[01:27] We can also pass the data between parent and child threads by using the scope to values.

[01:44] and drawbacks.
[01:45] By using these scope to values the Java team, they're trying to overcome the challenges around the
[01:50] thread local.

[01:56] But before that, let's try to understand what are the various options that we developers has to pass

LECTURE: [JAVA 25] Performance improvements using AOT - Theory
----------------------------------------

[00:00] Java team introduced some performance improvements by using aortic concept as part of Java 24 and 25
[00:09] release.
[00:10] Before I try to explain about these new features, first let me explain you on what is this Aot and
[00:18] how it is going to work.
[00:19] Aot means ahead of time.
[00:21] First, let's try to understand what is traditionally is going to happen when we start a Java application.
[00:28] When I say Java application, it can be a Java class or it can be a spring boot application, or it
[00:33] can be Java based application.
[00:35] For example, here I'm trying to run a Java class by using the Java My app command.
[00:40] Usually this command we can execute after we are done with the compilation by using the Java Sea command.
[00:47] When we are running this command behind the scenes, the JVM is going to start and it is going to read
[00:53] the Java files from the jar files.
[00:56] Because even though you are executing a simple Java class behind the scenes, the Java library.
[01:02] It is going to have a good amount of jar files, so all of them will be loaded from the disk.
[01:08] And in case if you're trying to run spring boot based applications or any other framework based applications
[01:15] in those scenarios, also all the Java related Jar files and framework related Jar files, they will
[01:21] be loaded from the disk.
[01:22] So once the Jar files are loaded from the disk, these jar files, they are going to have thousands
[01:28] of Java classes.
[01:30] All these Java classes will be parsed by the JVM one by one.
[01:35] Once the Java classes are parsed as part of the next step, all these classes will be loaded into the
[01:41] memory of your system or the server.
[01:43] So as part of this step, what is going to happen?
[01:45] All the Java class, they are going to be present inside the bytecode.
[01:48] All this bytecode will be converted into machine code.
[01:52] So this machine code will be dependent on the operating system.
[01:56] If you are using windows the corresponding conversion will happen.
[02:00] Otherwise if it is Mac.
[02:01] Accordingly, the conversion from bytecode to machine code will happen once all the classes are loaded
[02:08] into the memory.
[02:09] The links between the classes.
[02:11] Like we know, inside Java a class can be dependent on another class, so those links will be resolved
[02:18] along with the references.
[02:19] Followed by the JVM is going to run static initializers and towards the end the application is going
[02:25] to start.
[02:26] So this is going to happen every time you try to start your Java class or you try to start your Java
[02:32] application, but with the help of ahead of time approach, what is going to happen is we're going to
[02:38] do the task, like reading jar files from disk and parsing class files and loading class into memory
[02:43] and link classes together.
[02:45] So the step 234, five will only happen once, and it can be reused many times.
[02:52] To get the benefits of this Aot approach.
[02:55] First we need to run that training step.
[02:59] As part of this training step, we are going to run the application once and record what is going to
[03:04] happen as part of this.
[03:05] Step 2345.
[03:08] So whatever we recorded as part of the step two by using this preload and pre linking logic.
[03:14] So all those data will be saved into a cache file.
[03:18] Once we have this cache file ready.
[03:20] After executing this training run from next time onwards when we are trying to start the application,
[03:27] we can give the instructions to the JVM to use this cache file that was prepared in the training phase.
[03:34] So when the JVM is using this cache file, it is not going to execute these two, three, four, five
[03:40] steps one more time.
[03:41] And with that, what is going to happen?
[03:43] The startup time of the application is going to be improved, which results into much faster startup.
